fullParagraphs: India must shore up its partnerships in the Asian region

Each year, the summits of the 11-member Association of South-East Asian Nations mark an important moment on the diplomatic calendar: India is able to interact with all of its partners in the Indo-Pacific and engage global powers at the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s talks with Indo-Pacific players focused on a future shaped “not by competition, but by cooperation”. This year, the summit in Manila hosted by the Philippines had many other imperatives. These were the first ASEAN summits since the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran and Iran’s Hormuz blockade and strikes on Gulf countries that have upended energy and trade across South and South East Asia. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for “peace, stability, and predictability” in the world during the EAS was aimed as much at leaders from the U.S., Russia and China as it was for the region. The visit had a bilateral context — the Philippines and India have intensified ties considerably in the past year, since the visit of President Bongbong Marcos to Delhi in August 2025, including the upgradation of the Strategic Partnership, maritime exchanges and negotiations over the supply of more Indian-made Brahmos missile battery systems to the Philippines. This year, after months of concerns about U.S. President Donald Trump’s lack of interest in the Quad grouping, the U.S. decided to host a summit of U.S.-India-Australia-Japan Quad leaders on the side-lines of the ASEAN summits, the first time the summit has been held in a non-Quad country.

Given the stakes, there were several outcomes from all the three summits that PM Modi attended back-to-back on Tuesday — the ASEAN India Summit launched a new cooperation on disaster management, and the East Asia Summit focused on countering cyber-crime. PM Modi’s announcement that India would give all ASEAN citizens free tourist visas is expected to increase people-to-people interactions and trade. At the Quad summit, President Trump made a number of announcements including the launch of a Quad Business leaders forum, to be held in Mumbai next year, and the first Quad naval exercises with patrol aircraft. However, the outcomes in Manila paled in significance to the anticipation over Mr. Trump’s next stop in Shenzhen for the Asia Pacific Economic Conference (APEC), with an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping planned on Thursday. New Delhi must watch the outcomes of that summit among the “global superpowers” much more closely.

articles.title: Testing times: On India’s two-Test series against New Zealand
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand

New Zealand at home remains an indomitable cricketing opposition. Even the great West Indian squad led by Clive Lloyd suffered a 0-1 Test series defeat in 1980. Pitches that look lush as English meadows, the wind that is often bone-chilling cold, and fast bowlers relishing their prospects, make any tour of New Zealand a difficult outing. So far, the visiting Indians have done well, having won the T20I and ODI series, but the real contest starts with the first Test at Wellington’s Basin Reserve from Thursday. The Shubman Gill-led men’s last overseas tour of Sri Lanka ended with a middling 1-0 victory in the two Tests, but more needs to be done against New Zealand in the latest two-Test series. Placed fourth in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) table, and with hopes of securing a final berth seemingly fragile, India is in a win-all-games situation first up against New Zealand and later when Australia arrives next year. Against current WTC topper New Zealand, the Indian batters have to stay anchored. This is a line-up that no longer has Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane. Gill and company get another opportunity to reiterate their credentials.

For some rugged inspiration they need not look beyond coach Gautam Gambhir in their dressing room. The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.

articles.summary: India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand
articles.keyPoints:
• India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand
• New Zealand at home remains an indomitable cricketing opposition. Even the great West Indian squad led by Clive Lloyd suffered a 0-1 Test series defeat in 1980. Pitches that look lush as English meadows, the wind that is often bone-chilling cold, and fast bowlers relishing their prospects, make any tour of New Zealand a difficult outing. So far, the visiting Indians have done well, having won the T20I and ODI series, but the real contest starts with the first Test at Wellington’s Basin Reserve from Thursday. The Shubman Gill-led men’s last overseas tour of Sri Lanka ended with a middling 1-0 victory in the two Tests, but more needs to be done against New Zealand in the latest two-Test series. Placed fourth in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) table, and with hopes of securing a final berth seemingly fragile, India is in a win-all-games situation first up against New Zealand and later when Australia arrives next year. Against current WTC topper New Zealand, the Indian batters have to stay anchored. This is a line-up that no longer has Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane. Gill and company get another opportunity to reiterate their credentials.
• For some rugged inspiration they need not look beyond coach Gautam Gambhir in their dressing room. The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.

fullParagraphs: Restoration of Statehood is essential for peace in Jammu and Kashmir

Three months of lull established by security forces in Jammu and Kashmir was rattled by the back-to-back incidents of violence in the past six days. On November 11, a terror attack on a checkpoint manned by the personnel of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) in Kulgam left three jawans injured. On November 16, a local, whom the police suspected of having joined the terror ranks a few days ago, was killed after six days of a siege-like anti-terror operation in residential areas of Kulgam. In Jammu’s Kishtwar, two Special Police Officers (SPOs) of the J&K Police were found dead with bullet wounds, a day after they were reported missing in a forest range on November 11. The police and the Army, however, remain tight-lipped about the circumstances around the killing of these SPOs, and there are conflicting reports on the circumstances that led to their deaths. The anti-terror operation in civilian areas of Kulgam has raised concerns. Former J&K Chief Minister and PDP president Mehbooba Mufti described the operation, spread over six days, as “collective punishment that only breeds alienation and resentment,” while NC spokesman Imran Nabi Dar suggested that entire villages were put under prolonged restrictions for days. The Omar Abdullah government , because of limited powers and no jurisdiction over the police in J&K, a Union Territory since 2019, finds itself hamstrung. The iron hand policy to stamp out terrorism and separatism has been effective from a strictly security perspective — terror attacks as well as local recruitments into terror ranks have declined. According to the police, local recruits have come down to single digit or fewer than 10 in Kashmir.

That said, the decline in terrorist incidents and the silence of the streets should not be mistaken for peace. The current situation demands a political reach-out by the Centre to all the stakeholders of J&K. It has to begin with the much-promised restoration of Statehood , which will give the voters a sense that their mass participation in the 2024 Assembly elections allowed their elected leaders to hold institutions accountable, and they were able to work freely to protect the interests of the region. Though the security agencies need to be focused on Pakistan-backed terrorism, it should not come at the cost of re-inflicting psychological scars within Kashmir, which could turn into a powder keg if left unattended. Healing through both political and security processes has to be complementary rather than conflicting. Allowing the political class of J&K to establish its writ and providing room to security agencies to combat challenges are not contradictory.

articles.title: All-too fallible: On India’s vote against moratorium on death penalty
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Death penalty requires a near-infallible criminal justice system

India’s vote against a proposed global moratorium on the death penalty at the UN is consistent with its position at the forum; it has defended its retention of the penalty as a sovereign decision backed by judicial safeguards, including the “rarest of rare” condition and sessions courts’ sentences requiring a High Court’s confirmation. At the same time, the Supreme Court has increasingly restricted capital punishment and research has failed to find evidence of additional deterrence over life imprisonment . India’s distinction between judicial executions and extrajudicial killings is legally valid but its further claim that due process protects people facing execution is less so. While India last executed convicts in 2020, for the Delhi gang-rape and murder, Parliament expanded the number of capital offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — a form of penal populism that projects the political attractiveness of the state’s response to public outrage, especially in cases of sexual violence, without addressing the poor policing and low conviction rates that actually undermine deterrence . The country had 574 people on death row on December 31, 2025, the highest since 2016, thanks to trial court rulings, challenging claims about judicial safeguards in practice. The report of the 2015 Law Commission headed by Justice A.P. Shah said the death penalty “fails to achieve any constitutionally valid penological goals” and recommended abolishing it for all crimes except terrorism and waging war.

Only a small group of countries worldwide are executing more people. In India, per Project 39A, the Supreme Court released 38 persons from death row in 2016-2025 after they had spent eight years there on average. Some have endured more than two decades. The punishment requires a measure of infallibility that the criminal justice system cannot supply. The safeguards neither deter convictions in cases with flawed evidence, false testimony, and so on nor remedy unequal access to competent legal representation among those facing the penalty. India should formally suspend executions and commission a review of penalty statutes and the treatment of prisoners on death row. Second, it should spare offences that do not involve intentional killing from the penalty. Research suggests meting out excessively harsh punishments for non-fatal crimes could incentivise offenders to escalate their violence, including to kill potential witnesses. The greater goal should be to abolish the practice in law while improving investigative and prosecutorial practices and access to legal aid.

• Death penalty requires a near-infallible criminal justice system
• India’s vote against a proposed global moratorium on the death penalty at the UN is consistent with its position at the forum; it has defended its retention of the penalty as a sovereign decision backed by judicial safeguards, including the “rarest of rare” condition and sessions courts’ sentences requiring a High Court’s confirmation. At the same time, the Supreme Court has increasingly restricted capital punishment and research has failed to find evidence of additional deterrence over life imprisonment . India’s distinction between judicial executions and extrajudicial killings is legally valid but its further claim that due process protects people facing execution is less so. While India last executed convicts in 2020, for the Delhi gang-rape and murder, Parliament expanded the number of capital offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — a form of penal populism that projects the political attractiveness of the state’s response to public outrage, especially in cases of sexual violence, without addressing the poor policing and low conviction rates that actually undermine deterrence . The country had 574 people on death row on December 31, 2025, the highest since 2016, thanks to trial court rulings, challenging claims about judicial safeguards in practice. The report of the 2015 Law Commission headed by Justice A.P. Shah said the death penalty “fails to achieve any constitutionally valid penological goals” and recommended abolishing it for all crimes except terrorism and waging war.
• Only a small group of countries worldwide are executing more people. In India, per Project 39A, the Supreme Court released 38 persons from death row in 2016-2025 after they had spent eight years there on average. Some have endured more than two decades. The punishment requires a measure of infallibility that the criminal justice system cannot supply. The safeguards neither deter convictions in cases with flawed evidence, false testimony, and so on nor remedy unequal access to competent legal representation among those facing the penalty. India should formally suspend executions and commission a review of penalty statutes and the treatment of prisoners on death row. Second, it should spare offences that do not involve intentional killing from the penalty. Research suggests meting out excessively harsh punishments for non-fatal crimes could incentivise offenders to escalate their violence, including to kill potential witnesses. The greater goal should be to abolish the practice in law while improving investigative and prosecutorial practices and access to legal aid.

articles.title: Outlook outage: On Microsoft and dangers of centralising digital systems
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The dangers of centralising the internet’s architecture are now clear

Last week, Microsoft’s suite of productivity and email software, which businesses, governments, hospitals and a host of other organisations rely upon round-the-clock, abruptly stopped working globally , affecting tens of millions of people around the world. The company has cited a network upgrade gone awry as the root cause of the incident. Incidents such as the Microsoft 365 outage are a natural consequence of businesses and governments allowing key digital systems to become centralised all over the world. The internet remains, and was pioneered as, a network of networks. If one business’s networks went down, the reasoning went, others would not fall like dominos: everyone was, after all, connected to everyone else. But the economics have long been prohibitive, with dedicated servers and web-connected infrastructure infeasible for all but the largest businesses, with even those firms seeking the enticing cost savings from socialised infrastructure. That made sense: the internet made shared infrastructure more economical, allowing hardware and maintenance costs to be spread so far and wide that at a per-user level prices have been negligible. Competition among major cloud providers, the few that remain at Microsoft’s scale, have kept prices affordable for enterprise software for all shades of organisations.

Digital services have grown more sophisticated, and more deeply integrated into the economy as this centralisation unfolded. But the downside is that, regardless of the sophistication and professionalism of any company, mistakes happen, and the scale of these mistakes can quickly cascade over to the entire economy. There are societal and organisational lessons to be gleaned from these episodes. There is no such thing as a reliable vendor. Governments must also draw a cyber sovereignty lesson here that does not simply entail swapping a global vendor for a domestic one. It is the subversion of the internet’s architecture that is at the root of these incidents. Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems. As a new generation of AI data centres is poised to supercharge the centralised systems of yesteryear, it is all the more imperative to mitigate even occasional vagaries of large systems.

articles.title: Clear the path: On SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India should use multilateral fora to advance bilateral cooperation

While maintaining its hard stance on cross-border terrorism, India has an opportunity to recognise that many of its other interests still merit sustained cooperation with Pakistan as the latter’s climate minister Musadik Masood Malik prepares to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi. India’s official position since the Pahalgam attack and the ensuing confrontations along the border is that terrorism and bilateral talks cannot coexist. A month later, Prime Minister Narendra Modi signalled that India’s relations with Pakistan would remain subordinate to its demands on cross-border terrorism by extending the condition to trade and water. South Asia is already one of the least economically integrated regions worldwide, with intra-regional trade at around 5%, and, as Chatham House has inferred, strained ties between India and its neighbours have created diplomatic vacuums that Beijing has taken advantage of through trilateral and regional groupings. Now, by inviting all SCO members to the national capital and participating in meetings ahead of the August 2027 Islamabad Summit, New Delhi has shown some maturity as a convening power. Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Mr. Modi.

The pursuit of regionwide water security remains particularly fluid, with India seemingly overlooking the fact that it is upstream of Pakistan and Bangladesh and downstream of China. After India stopped sharing routine hydrological data of the Indus river and approved the Chenab-Beas link tunnel project, Mr. Malik fanned the flames saying Pakistan would “cut off those hands” seeking to restrict its share of the water. Yet China has now restricted the same data vis-à-vis the Brahmaputra while it builds the Medog mega-dam in Tibet. India has also protested the proposed Padma Barrage in Bangladesh, which has been increasing its alignment with China, echoing India building the Farakka Barrage over East Pakistan’s objections in 1961. Climate change is rendering cooperation more essential to manage the integrity of contested geographies, the willingness of border populations to engage, and the potential to generate hydroelectric power. New Delhi should retreat from the notion that working together on the Indus will be a concession to Islamabad and see in the Dialogue an opportunity to restore the necessary channels. Suspending ties may communicate political resolve but will not diminish terrorists’ capabilities in the region or improve India’s security. It has already compromised India’s ambitions to regional leadership, which require the ability to keep engaging even with difficult neighbours. India should go beyond using multilateral fora to assert its national position and start identifying areas where bilateral cooperation serves its interests, including with Pakistan.

articles.title: Madurai Bench of Madras High Court directs T.N. government not to open any new Tasmac shops
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: A Division Bench said the State already had a large number of Tasmac shops, and considering the public interest, new Tasmac shops should not be opened
The Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court on Wednesday directed the State government not to open any new Tasmac liquor shops in Tamil Nadu.
A Division Bench of Justices P. Velmurugan and K.K. Ramakrishnan said the State already had a large number of Tasmac shops, and considering the public interest, new Tasmac shops should not be opened.
The court passed the direction while allowing a public interest litigation petition filed by V. Manikandan of Navakinathupatti in Nallampillai village in Tiruchi district.

The petitioner said about 30 families lived in the village, where agriculture was the predominant occupation. The authorities had proposed to establish a Tasmac shop at Navakinathupatti. He said school students pass through the proposed site to reach the government school at Karattupatti, and that the area was accident-prone.
The opening of a liquor shop in the area would affect the safety of women and the welfare of school students, he said. He pointed out that a Tasmac shop was already located in a nearby village.
He said there was no necessity or justification for establishing another liquor shop in the vicinity without assessing the existing outlet’s impact.

The residents had already requested the authorities not to establish any liquor shop in the village or in the surrounding villages, he said, seeking a direction to restrain the authorities from establishing the Tasmac shop.
The petitioner said he had made a detailed representation to the authorities concerned in this regard. However, no action had been taken so far.

articles.title: BJP turns to Mathura temple issue amid cadre unease, allies’ pressure
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Political observers say the renewed focus on Krishna Janmabhoomi serves as a “smokescreen” to mask simmering discontent among the party cadre over the UGC’s equity rules, SIR drive and seat sharing with alliance partners

Days after Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav made his ‘Dumdar Dalit’ outreach in Agra, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) responded on November 16 with ‘Radhe Radhe, Kamal Khila De’ and ‘Abki Baari Baanke Bihari’.

It was senior BJP leader and Deputy Chief Minister Keshav Prasad Maurya who spelt out to reporters, during the party’s two-day conclave in Mathura earlier this week, that constructing a grand temple at the Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi in Mathura would be at the centre of their campaign for the upcoming Uttar Pradesh Assembly election. The ruling party signalled that it would counter the SP’s ‘PDA’ [‘Pichhde’ (backward classes), Dalits and ‘Alpsankhyak’ (minorities)] card with the mantra of cultural nationalism, supplementing it with the ‘double-engine’ government’s “success stories” on the development and law and order fronts.

articles.title: India’s CSR spending leaves gaps in health, water security, innovation: Report
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), for instance, account for 60% of deaths in India, up from 45% in 2004-06. Yet, nearly 62% of identifiable NCD funding goes towards cancer, while cardiovascular diseases receive around 12%, despite accounting for over half of NCD deaths, says a study by a City-based global impact consulting firm

A significant share of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funding in India continues to flow towards established sectors, while several pressing development challenges receive comparatively limited attention, according to a report by Sattva Consulting and India Data Insights.
The analysis of CSR projects between FY23 and FY25 points to funding gaps in non-communicable diseases, women’s economic agency, school-to-work transition, groundwater resilience and innovation.

Nearly 80% of CSR funding is concentrated in five sectors, with education accounting for 35% and healthcare for 21%. However, the report finds gaps even within these established areas. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), for instance, account for 60% of deaths in India, up from 45% in 2004-06. Yet, nearly 62% of identifiable NCD funding goes towards cancer, while cardiovascular diseases receive around 12%, despite accounting for over half of the NCD deaths.

The report also points to a gap between education and employment outcomes. Youth unemployment stands at 9.9% rising to 25.9% among graduates. Of the CSR funding for the school-to-work transition, 42% goes towards academic and skilling support. For every rupee allocated to these areas, only 24 paise goes towards giving young people exposure to the world of work.

A similar concentration is visible in funding for women’s economic agency. The area receives ₹1,122.8 crore or 29% of identifiable women-focused CSR funding, with nearly 77% directed towards skilling and livelihoods. The report also highlights barriers such as inadequate care infrastructure, unsafe mobility and limited market access.

In groundwater resilience, Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana account for nearly 49% of India’s critical and over-exploited groundwater units, but receive only around 7% of identifiable CSR funding for the area.
Innovation and research also receive limited attention, with approximately ₹298 crore in CSR funding between FY23 and FY25. No industry directs more than 1.2% of its total CSR spending to this area.

“CSR has brought size and predictability to funding. It now needs agility. CSR cannot replace the government, but it can be patient and risk-tolerant in ways other capital often cannot. That allows it to test unproven models, build evidence on what works and help scale its adoption,” said Srikrishna Sridhar Murthy, co-founder and CEO of Sattva Consulting, a global impact consulting firm headquartered in Bengaluru.
“The question for corporates is no longer only how much they spend, but whether that spend is reaching the problems where it can make a difference,” Srikrishna added.
India’s annual CSR spending reached ₹40,794 crore in FY25, growing at 15% annually over the past decade.

articles.title: UEF, IIT-M join hands for Tamil Nadu Growth Conclave 2026; focus on 10 key sectors
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The United Economic Forum (UEF) Chamber of Commerce has signed an MoU with the Indian Institute of Technology - Madras (IIT-M) to collaborate for the Tamil Nadu Growth Conclave 2026 scheduled to be held on December 8, 2026. The objective of this MoU is to facilitate knowledge sharing, industry academia collaboration, innovation, investment and stakeholder engagement towards Tamil Nadu’s economic growth.

The event will focus on 10 sectors, including Automotive & EV; Electronics & Semiconductors; IT, AI and Digital; Advanced Engineering & Capital Goods; Textiles & Technical Textiles; Pharma, Biotech & MedTech; Agri & Food Processing; Renewable & Green Energy; Logistics, Ports & Global Trade and Aerospace & Defence. articles.title: Panjab University improves its global standing in interdisciplinary scientific research
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The 2027 edition of the rankings, produced by Times Higher Education in association with Schmidt Science Fellows, assessed 1,058 institutions across 102 countries and territories, compared with 911 institutions in the 2026 edition

Chandigarh-based Panjab University (PU) has improved its global standing in interdisciplinary scientific research, climbing 24 places to secure the joint 150th position in the Times Higher Education (THE) Interdisciplinary Science Rankings 2027. The University’s overall score has increased to 55.0 from 52.8 in 2026 and 48.6 in 2025.

In a statement on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), Vice-Chancellor Meenakshi Goyal said, “This improvement in Panjab University’s global standing reflects our continued commitment to strengthening interdisciplinary research and academic collaboration. It is the outcome of the collective efforts of our faculty, researchers, students, and staff. We will continue to build an enabling research ecosystem that encourages collaboration across disciplines, supports innovation, and addresses complex societal challenges aimed at Viksit Bharat through knowledge and research.”

The 2027 edition of the rankings, produced by Times Higher Education in association with Schmidt Science Fellows, assessed 1,058 institutions across 102 countries and territories, compared with 911 institutions in the 2026 edition. A total of 565 Asian institutions were ranked, up from 478 last year.

The Interdisciplinary Science Rankings assess universities’ contributions and commitment to research that brings together knowledge and methods from different academic disciplines to address complex challenges. The rankings cover collaborations involving multiple scientific disciplines as well as research combining scientific disciplines with areas such as the social sciences, education, psychology, law, economics, and clinical and health studies.

articles.title: India’s Oct. crude import bill soars 87.5% to $19.5-bn amid West Asia tensions, volumes up 11%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: While higher petroleum product exports offer a partial natural hedge, sustained increases in crude and gas prices could intensify pressure on the country’s import bill.

India’s crude oil import bill surged 87.5% year-on-year (YoY) to $19.5 billion in October, as elevated international benchmark prices, fuelled by renewed tensions in West Asia, sharply increased procurement costs. The increase came alongside an 11% rise in import volumes.

The net import bill, calculated as imports of crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas less exports of petroleum products, rose 60% to $16 billion during the month, compared with $10 billion in October last year.
Higher export realisations from petroleum products, however, provided some cushion against the escalating import burden.

According to provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), India imported 23.3 million metric tonnes (MMT) of crude oil in October, against 21 MMT in the corresponding month last year.
The expenditure on crude imports, meanwhile, climbed to $19.5 billion from $10.4 billion, reflecting the disproportionate impact of higher international prices on the country’s energy import bill.

The Indian crude oil basket averaged $119.91 per barrel in October, compared with $124.77 per barrel for Brent crude. In September, the Indian basket had averaged $116.09 per barrel, while Brent stood at $116.77 per barrel.

The sustained increase in benchmark prices, amid continuing geopolitical uncertainties in West Asia, has left India exposed to higher energy procurement costs, given its dependence on imported crude oil.
The impact of the rising crude import bill was partly offset by stronger earnings from petroleum product exports.
India’s petroleum product exports increased 5.9% in volume terms to 5.4 MMT in October. However, export revenues surged approximately 91% to $6.3 billion.
The increase in export earnings provided an important buffer against the higher cost of crude procurement.

📈 Economic, Banking & Finance 📅 18 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 2 Min Read

📰 India’s Oct. crude import bill soars 87.5% to $19.5-bn amid West Asia tensions, volumes up 11%

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance

While higher petroleum product exports offer a partial natural hedge, sustained increases in crude and gas prices could intensify pressure on the country’s import bill.

India’s crude oil import bill surged 87.5% year-on-year (YoY) to $19.5 billion in October, as elevated international benchmark prices, fuelled by renewed tensions in West Asia, sharply increased procurement costs. The increase came alongside an 11% rise in import volumes.

The net import bill, calculated as imports of crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas less exports of petroleum products, rose 60% to $16 billion during the month, compared with $10 billion in October last year.

Higher export realisations from petroleum products, however, provided some cushion against the escalating import burden.

According to provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), India imported 23.3 million metric tonnes (MMT) of crude oil in October, against 21 MMT in the corresponding month last year.

The expenditure on crude imports, meanwhile, climbed to $19.5 billion from $10.4 billion, reflecting the disproportionate impact of higher international prices on the country’s energy import bill.

The Indian crude oil basket averaged $119.91 per barrel in October, compared with $124.77 per barrel for Brent crude. In September, the Indian basket had averaged $116.09 per barrel, while Brent stood at $116.77 per barrel.

The sustained increase in benchmark prices, amid continuing geopolitical uncertainties in West Asia, has left India exposed to higher energy procurement costs, given its dependence on imported crude oil.

The impact of the rising crude import bill was partly offset by stronger earnings from petroleum product exports.

India’s petroleum product exports increased 5.9% in volume terms to 5.4 MMT in October. However, export revenues surged approximately 91% to $6.3 billion.

The increase in export earnings provided an important buffer against the higher cost of crude procurement.

articles.title: India-U.S. trade deal signing will still ‘take some time’, says Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: He added that the deal can be signed only after the U.S. finalises its new tariff framework. Recently, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the two nations had agreed that India would receive an advantage over its competitors

The actual signing of the India-U.S. trade will still “take some time”, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), adding that the negotiation part and the legal text will be completed soon.

The delay in signing, he said, was because it can be done only after the U.S. concludes its Section 301 investigations into its trade partners and finalises its tariff structure. A few days ago, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal asserted that the U.S. has acknowledged that India will receive lower tariffs as compared to its competitors.

“This is a deal that has been announced in February, the contours have already been announced as part of the joint statement,” Mr. Agrawal said while speaking at the curtain raiser of the FICCI Annual General Meeting. “The legal agreement has also been negotiated and it is now in final stages and it will be concluded soon.”
He was referring to the joint statement between India and the U.S. in February that announced the framework of an interim deal on trade.

However, Mr. Agrawal explained that the “challenge” is that this framework was announced against the background of the executive tariffs system that the U.S. President Donald Trump had put in place. At the time, the tariff on India was 50%. Later in February, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the legal foundation of these tariffs.

“Now a new tariff architecture is being created by the U.S.,” Mr. Agrawal explained. “So until that tariff architecture comes back in place, the signing of a deal is something that I think will take some time. But concluding the negotiations and having everything ready will be something that we will strive to achieve as soon as possible.”
In particular, Mr. Agrawal spoke about the investigations undertaken by the American administration under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

One of these investigations, regarding forced labour, has been completed and a tariff of 10% has been levied on imports from India. The second investigation, looking into excess capacity, is yet to be completed and could come with further tariffs.

“There are certain 301 investigations which are already under review,” Mr. Agrawal said. “Those will also be coming to the fore in the next few weeks or months. You can’t have a deal until you have got uncertainty around multiple investigations which are already there.”

Separately, without mentioning the U.S. or any other country, Mr. Agrawal also asserted that trade deals can take a long time to conclude when parties try to maximise the benefits accruing to them rather than engaging in a spirit of compromise.

articles.title: Rising prices reflect government’s economic mismanagement: Congress
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Monthly costs up by over 20% for 61% of families, according to a survey cited by Congress leader Jairam Ramesh; claims PM is more pre-occupied with politics than tackling the inflation crisis

The Congress on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) accused the Union government of fuelling inflation through its “economic mismanagement and anti-people policies” and alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi remained preoccupied with politics rather than addressing the economic distress faced by households and businesses.

Congress general secretary (communications) Jairam Ramesh cited a survey which found that, for 61% of families across the country, monthly household expenditure had risen by more than 20% over the past year. While 74% of respondents were cutting back on non-essential spending, 50% had reduced purchases of essential goods, he said.
Citing the survey, Mr. Ramesh said prices of ghee and edible oils had risen by 75%, vegetables by 73%, cereals by 71%, milk and dairy products by 65%, and pulses by 62%.

He also claimed that 200 garment factories had shut down in Noida over the past year, citing the impact of U.S. tariffs, high input costs, and government apathy. He said the closures reflected the wider distress in the textile industry.

“People’s plates are shrinking, and factories are being locked down. Yet, the Prime Minister’s only concern remains politics,” he said on X, accusing the government of failing to acknowledge people’s hardships or offer relief.

articles.title: U.S., Venezuela sign deal to re-establish military ties: Hegseth
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The U.S. Defence Secretary said that following the January capture of Nicolas Maduro by the U.S. military, the country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner”
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking in Venezuela, said the two countries have signed an agreement to re-establish military ties, from training to intelligence sharing.

Mr. Hegseth said that following the January capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro by the U.S. military, the country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner.”
Mr. Hegseth also praised the “close cooperation” with interim President Delcy Rodriguez that allowed officials “to stabilise Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all.”
The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.

Ms. Rodríguez separately lauded the opportunity to strengthen the military partnership. “I hope that this technical-military cooperation … can be brought to its highest possible level so that ... we may address common threats,” she said.
Mr. Hegseth’s visit underscores efforts by President Donald Trump’s administration to deepen its influence in the South American country since U.S. forces ousted Maduro in January.

Mr. Hegseth is the latest member of Mr. Trump’s Cabinet to travel to Venezuela following visits this year by the Interior and Energy secretaries, who have focused on efforts to tap its oil reserves and critical minerals. Mr. Trump said in August that Mr. Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves.
The head of U.S. military operations in Latin America, Gen. Francis Donovan of U.S. Southern Command, also has met interim authorities in Venezuela at least twice this year.

The U.S. military has been expanding its attention on the region since Mr. Trump returned to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the Western Hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels.

To try to stem the flow of narcotics into the U.S. and the scourge of fatal overdoses, American forces have been attacking what the Trump administration says are boats smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” in September 2025, although U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims the vessels were carrying drugs.

articles.title: UN Sustainable Development Goals group for science, technology rejigged
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The group has been constituted even as the international community ramps up efforts to achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development

The United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has reconstituted a 10-member group that works on promoting science, technology and innovation toward achieving its Sustainable Development Goals. The lone Indian in this group is former biologist and former Council of Scientific and Industrial Research CSIR Director General, Shekhar Mande, who is also currently President, Indian National Science Academy.
The group has been constituted even as the international community ramps up efforts to achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, while preparing for the 2027 SDG Summit.

“The group comprises distinguished experts from diverse geographic and disciplinary backgrounds from both developing and developed countries. Each member, recognised for their international excellence in science or technology, brings a wealth of experience and insight from civil society, the private sector, and the scientific community, underscoring the inclusive and comprehensive approach the UN is taking towards sustainable development,” an accompanying press statement noted.

The other members of the group are Marian Dorcas Quain (Ghana), Deputy Director-General of CSIR Ghana; Giorgio Rossi (Italy), Vice-President of Elettra-Sincrotrone Trieste; Magnus Andersson (Sweden), Associate Professor at Malmö University; Mônica Tejo Cavalcanti (Brazil), Professor at the Federal University of Campina Grande; Evgeniya Dmitrieva (Russia), Member of the Civic Chamber of the Russian Federation; Motoko Kotani (Japan), Executive Director of Science at RIKEN; Jin Li (China), President of Fudan University; Madin Maseeh (Maldives), President of the Maldives Space Research Organisation; and Rita Orji (Nigeria), Canada Research Chair in Persuasive Technology at Dalhousie University.
Professor Mande is also President of Vijnana Bharti, which, along with the Ministry of Science and Technology is gearing up to host the India International Science Festival in Pune in December.

Announcing this on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), Union Minister of Science Jitendra Singh said at a press briefing that the government had taken a conscious decision to replace “scattered, repetitive gatherings”, including the erstwhile Indian Science Congress, with two flagship national events carrying distinct identities.

While the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave in October saw 13 Ministries and Nobel Laureates, and was an academic-driven conclave exploring frontier themes, the India International Science Festival (IISF) brought a “festive, public-facing character with international resonance”. By rotating the venue to different regions, after Chandigarh, Hyderabad, Goa and Delhi, bringing IISF for the first time to Pune leverages the western hub’s vibrant academic, research, and industrial ecosystem.

articles.title: Saudis prepare for Houthi war to last well into 2027
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Saudi and Yemeni forces are ​now reorganising, with plans to protect Aden from the Houthi advances and potentially shift their offensive to eastern fronts where they have made some advances or have at least held their lines

Saudi Arabia is preparing for war against Yemen's Houthis to stretch well into next year, doubling down despite setbacks on the battlefield in Yemen ​and attacks disrupting life at home, said two Western officials briefed by Saudis on the plans.

The renewed conflict has become the most active front in ‌the wider Iran war, killing and wounding thousands and displacing hundreds of thousands in Yemen while derailing ​Saudi Arabia's efforts to draw in non-oil investment and host global events.
Public messaging around the war has also ⁠slowly shifted in the kingdom, with greater acknowledgement of its impacts.

Saudi officials now foresee the campaign stretching on for up to six months, aiming to see gains on the ground by the kingdom's Yemeni allies before any negotiations with the Houthis, according to Western officials, who spoke on condition ‌of anonymity to discuss non-public conversations with Saudi counterparts.
A third source familiar with the Saudi plans confirmed the accounts. All three said a deal to end the wider Iran war could see the Yemen conflict draw down.

The ‌third source also said Riyadh believes that U.S. offensive support for Saudi operations in Yemen, which President Donald Trump's administration has ‌so ⁠far withheld, could help change the tide of the conflict, potentially allowing Saudi-backed forces to make the gains ⁠they want within weeks.
A Saudi Foreign Ministry official declined to comment on the views of Saudi officials as described by the Western officials.

Saudi Arabia first entered the Yemen conflict in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to restore Yemen's government to power after the Houthis seized the ​capital Sanaa and much of the country. They fought to ‌a bloody stalemate and in 2022 reached a ceasefire that lasted until summer this year.

Since fighting restarted, the Houthis have seized the Red Sea coast and strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait from Saudi-backed forces, and encircled the city of Taiz in highlands above the government's temporary capital Aden on the southern coast.
Yemeni government forces mounted a counterattack last month, recapturing territory around the ‌strait, but withdrew over the past weekend to protect Aden in a major setback.

articles.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea amass forces along border, heightening war fears: Sources
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The fighting in Tigray has stoked fears of a ​wider conflagration in the Horn of Africa, with Ethiopia’s government also accusing Sudan, which is in the midst of its own civil war, and Egypt of backing the rebels; Eritrea, Sudan, Egypt ⁠all deny doing so

Ethiopia and Eritrea have amassed forces along their shared border, conflict monitors and people tied to militias in northern Ethiopia's Tigray ‌region said, fuelling fears of outright war between the historical rivals.

The build-up along the border has brought ​the two armies within striking distance of each other, according to the conflict monitors ACLED and the International ⁠Crisis Group, a person close to a pro-Ethiopian government militia in Tigray, and another person close to anti-government rebels there.

Reuters could not independently confirm reports of skirmishes between Ethiopian and Eritrean forces along the border. ACLED and a person close to the rebels said the ‌two sides had clashed in recent days, which would be their first direct armed exchanges in over a month, but the person close to the pro-Ethiopian government militia disputed this.

Reached for comment, Eritrean Information ‌Minister Yemane Gebremeskel decried "propaganda" from Ethiopia's ruling party about developments near the border but did not directly address reports about ‌military ⁠build-ups or clashes.
Spokespeople for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Diplomats and ⁠experts have warned of possible conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea since fighting broke out in September between Ethiopia’s federal government and rebels in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.

Witnesses and Ethiopia's government said Eritrean forces crossed into Tigray in early October in support ​of the rebels. ACLED reported at the time ‌that drone strikes it believed were carried out by Ethiopia’s military had targeted the Eritrean troops. Ethiopia has not commented on the strikes.

Eritrea has denied any incursion into Ethiopia and accused Addis Ababa of seeking a pretext to invade its smaller neighbour, which was an Ethiopian province for three decades before gaining independence in 1993. They are now separated ‌by a border stretching more than 1,000 km (620 miles).

The fighting in Tigray has stoked fears of a ​wider conflagration in the Horn of Africa, with Ethiopia’s government also accusing Sudan, which is in the midst of its own civil war, and Egypt of backing the rebels. Eritrea, Sudan, and Egypt ⁠all deny doing so.

Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 that killed tens of thousands of people. The conflict was prompted by a dispute over the border town of Badme, which a UN boundary commission later found fell within Eritrean ‌territory.

Spokespeople for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Diplomats and ⁠experts have warned of possible conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea since fighting broke out in September between Ethiopia’s federal government and rebels in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace faults Israel, Hamas for failure to end Gaza war
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: While the ceasefire has halted major fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas ⁠to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect last year

The body overseeing U.S. President Donald Trump's plan to end the Gaza ‌war accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities, leaving ​the population of Gaza in dire conditions and the ceasefire in danger of collapse.

The 12-page Board ⁠of Peace report, seen by Reuters , is the body's second to the United Nations Security Council since the U.S.-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a sobering assessment of progress made since then.
The Board, established and headed by Mr. Trump, is expected ‌to present the report's findings to a meeting of the council in New York at the end of November.

"The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains ‌the principal risk to the process," the report said, warning that "a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be ‌sustained ⁠indefinitely."

While the ceasefire has halted major fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas ⁠to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect last year.

Hamas agreed in July to a Board of Peace roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel rejected ​the roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas ‌is dismantled.
Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, while the report said Hamas fighters have also continued attacks on Israeli troops.
"Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas' agreement to the roadmap to the test," the report said.
"Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not ‌been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble."

Senior Hamas ​official Basem Naim dismissed the report as "pure disinformation", accusing the Board of Peace of providing cover to Israel to evade its commitments under the plan to end the war and to ⁠continue its aggression in Gaza.

articles.title: COVID-19 lessons should inform response to air pollution
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Tackling air pollution already attracts considerable expenditure, but allocations do not consistently reflect the greatest health risks

There is an uncanny similarity between Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic, and air pollution. During the pandemic, the virus entered our bodies through the air we breathed; harmful particulate matter and toxic gases enter through the same respiratory route. Additionally, both damage multiple organs, including the lungs, heart and brain. Yet, while COVID-19 prompted an unprecedented emergency national response, air pollution continues to be treated largely as a seasonal inconvenience.

The harmful effects of air pollution are well-established. An adult takes approximately 20,000–25,000 breaths daily, meaning that even a relatively miniscule worsening of air quality can have substantial health consequences over time. This alone should make improving the quality of air an urgent public health priority.

Science, Space & Environment Report: COVID-19 lessons should inform response to air pollution. This milestone highlights indigenous research, technological self-reliance, and environmental sustainability.

articles.title: A regulatory fix for India’s campuses
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Ministry must act without delay and issue a statutory notification, consistent with the court’s judgment, for eligible educational campuses

India’s education infrastructure has always been the strongest foundation of its growth and development. However, recent Supreme Court judgments have reaffirmed that educational buildings exceeding 20,000 square metres require prior Environmental Clearance (EC) under the Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006. Institutions that have already constructed such buildings without obtaining clearance are now left without any procedure to secure it, creating a serious obstacle. The issue has developed because of two major regulatory changes.

Before the EIA Notification, 2006, there was no built-up-area-based EC requirement for educational institutions. The Notification brought large construction projects, including educational campuses, within the prior EC framework. In December 2014, the Union government exempted schools, colleges and institutional hostels from EC, subject to environmental management conditions. The Kerala High Court quashed this exemption in March 2024. The government introduced a fresh exemption in January 2025, but Vanashakti challenged it before the Supreme Court. After staying its operation, the court cancelled the exemption in August 2025. Consequently, large educational buildings again became subject to prior EC requirements.
Science, Space & Environment Report: A regulatory fix for India’s campuses. This milestone highlights indigenous research, technological self-reliance, and environmental sustainability.

articles.title: Construction activities on Kaziranga wildlife corridors flagged
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: An Eastern Assam-based environment activist writes to the Supreme Court-constituted Central Empowered Committee, highlighting the concerns

An eastern Assam-based environmental activist has reminded the Supreme Court–constituted Central Empowered Committee (CEC) to continue construction activities on the wildlife corridors of Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve.

Kaziranga has nine notified wildlife corridors and several dandis or animal pathways. Animals use these corridors and dandis mostly to escape to the hills of Karbi Anglong district when the park is flooded during the monsoon months.

In a letter to the CEC’s Member-Secretary on November 16, Rohit Choudhury said he had brought such construction activities to the notice of the Committee on May 11. He lamented the lack of action against these activities, violating the Supreme Court’s April 2019 order.

“We order that all kinds of mining and related activities along the aforesaid Kaziranga National Park area and in the entire catchment area of rivers, streams and rivulets originating in the Karbi Anglong Hill ranges and flowing into Kaziranga National Park, including the Tiger Reserve, are restrained. No new construction shall be permitted on private lands which form part of the nine identified animal corridors,” the apex court’s order read.

“Despite this clear and categorical prohibition, the Government of Assam has displayed a disturbing disregard for the mandate of the Supreme Court by permitting and facilitating unlawful construction activities within these ecologically sensitive wildlife corridors,” Mr. Choudhury wrote.

He reminded the CEC of photographic evidence of a building under construction on the Haldhibari Wildlife Corridor attached to his May 11 letter. “The construction activity was allowed to proceed unabated and has now reached an advanced stage of completion,” he wrote, attaching recent photographs of the construction site.

Mr. Choudhury said the CEC’s inability to take up the matter six months ago “effectively afforded the concerned authorities sufficient time to continue and substantially complete the illegal construction”.
He said such delays in addressing matters of grave environmental significance seriously undermine the purpose and efficacy of the CEC’s mandate.
The activist further said the CEC did not inform the Supreme Court of any violation of its April 12, 2019, order for necessary action.

“This persistent failure of enforcement has emboldened continued violations and weakened the protection envisaged by the Supreme Court,” he said, urging the CEC to recommend contempt proceedings against the officials responsible for permitting, facilitating or failing to prevent these blatant violations of the court’s binding directions.

articles.title: Scientists warn of growing health threats of chemicals found everywhere
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs
Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a "global and growing threat" to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned.

The report on "endocrine-disrupting chemicals" (EDCs) released by the United Nations Environment Programme and World Health Organization "conservatively" estimates the health and environmental costs of EDC exposure at over $1 trillion annually.

"The scientific evidence is clear: EDCs are a global and growing threat to human and environmental health," warns the report written by international scientists, calling current regulations "uneven and insufficient."
EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs.
They are in everything from toys and makeup, to building materials and clothing.
The report released late Tuesday is the first such comprehensive look at EDC impacts in 14 years, and finds increasingly clear links between them and a range of diseases.
"The evidence is so strong that it's irrefutable at this point," said Laura Vandenberg, report co-author and professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
The report examined thousands of studies on chemicals like bisphenols, phthalates and parabens.
Evidence of links between these chemicals and disease is strongest for certain neurological conditions and reproductive problems including sperm decline.
But there is also growing confidence that EDCs are linked to diseases like type 2 diabetes and asthma that have spiked globally.

articles.title: Many imperatives: On India’s Asia diplomacy
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India must shore up its partnerships in the Asian region

Each year, the summits of the 11-member Association of South-East Asian Nations mark an important moment on the diplomatic calendar: India is able to interact with all of its partners in the Indo-Pacific and engage global powers at the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s talks with Indo-Pacific players focused on a future shaped “not by competition, but by cooperation”. This year, the summit in Manila hosted by the Philippines had many other imperatives. These were the first ASEAN summits since the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran and Iran’s Hormuz blockade and strikes on Gulf countries that have upended energy and trade across South and South East Asia. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for “peace, stability, and predictability” in the world during the EAS was aimed as much at leaders from the U.S., Russia and China as it was for the region. The visit had a bilateral context — the Philippines and India have intensified ties considerably in the past year, since the visit of President Bongbong Marcos to Delhi in August 2025, including the upgradation of the Strategic Partnership, maritime exchanges and negotiations over the supply of more Indian-made Brahmos missile battery systems to the Philippines. This year, after months of concerns about U.S. President Donald Trump’s lack of interest in the Quad grouping, the U.S. decided to host a summit of U.S.-India-Australia-Japan Quad leaders on the side-lines of the ASEAN summits, the first time the summit has been held in a non-Quad country.

Given the stakes, there were several outcomes from all the three summits that PM Modi attended back-to-back on Tuesday — the ASEAN India Summit launched a new cooperation on disaster management, and the East Asia Summit focused on countering cyber-crime. PM Modi’s announcement that India would give all ASEAN citizens free tourist visas is expected to increase people-to-people interactions and trade. At the Quad summit, President Trump made a number of announcements including the launch of a Quad Business leaders forum, to be held in Mumbai next year, and the first Quad naval exercises with patrol aircraft. However, the outcomes in Manila paled in significance to the anticipation over Mr. Trump’s next stop in Shenzhen for the Asia Pacific Economic Conference (APEC), with an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping planned on Thursday. New Delhi must watch the outcomes of that summit among the “global superpowers” much more closely.

India must shore up its partnerships in the Asian region

Each year, the summits of the 11-member Association of South-East Asian Nations mark an important moment on the diplomatic calendar: India is able to interact with all of its partners in the Indo-Pacific and engage global powers at the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s talks with Indo-Pacific players focused on a future shaped “not by competition, but by cooperation”. This year, the summit in Manila hosted by the Philippines had many other imperatives. These were the first ASEAN summits since the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran and Iran’s Hormuz blockade and strikes on Gulf countries that have upended energy and trade across South and South East Asia. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for “peace, stability, and predictability” in the world during the EAS was aimed as much at leaders from the U.S., Russia and China as it was for the region. The visit had a bilateral context — the Philippines and India have intensified ties considerably in the past year, since the visit of President Bongbong Marcos to Delhi in August 2025, including the upgradation of the Strategic Partnership, maritime exchanges and negotiations over the supply of more Indian-made Brahmos missile battery systems to the Philippines. This year, after months of concerns about U.S. President Donald Trump’s lack of interest in the Quad grouping, the U.S. decided to host a summit of U.S.-India-Australia-Japan Quad leaders on the side-lines of the ASEAN summits, the first time the summit has been held in a non-Quad country.

Given the stakes, there were several outcomes from all the three summits that PM Modi attended back-to-back on Tuesday — the ASEAN India Summit launched a new cooperation on disaster management, and the East Asia Summit focused on countering cyber-crime. PM Modi’s announcement that India would give all ASEAN citizens free tourist visas is expected to increase people-to-people interactions and trade. At the Quad summit, President Trump made a number of announcements including the launch of a Quad Business leaders forum, to be held in Mumbai next year, and the first Quad naval exercises with patrol aircraft. However, the outcomes in Manila paled in significance to the anticipation over Mr. Trump’s next stop in Shenzhen for the Asia Pacific Economic Conference (APEC), with an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping planned on Thursday. New Delhi must watch the outcomes of that summit among the “global superpowers” much more closely.

articles.title: Testing times: On India’s two-Test series against New Zealand
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India needs to be at its best in Tests against New Zealand

New Zealand at home remains an indomitable cricketing opposition. Even the great West Indian squad led by Clive Lloyd suffered a 0-1 Test series defeat in 1980. Pitches that look lush as English meadows, the wind that is often bone-chilling cold, and fast bowlers relishing their prospects, make any tour of New Zealand a difficult outing. So far, the visiting Indians have done well, having won the T20I and ODI series, but the real contest starts with the first Test at Wellington’s Basin Reserve from Thursday. The Shubman Gill-led men’s last overseas tour of Sri Lanka ended with a middling 1-0 victory in the two Tests, but more needs to be done against New Zealand in the latest two-Test series. Placed fourth in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) table, and with hopes of securing a final berth seemingly fragile, India is in a win-all-games situation first up against New Zealand and later when Australia arrives next year. Against current WTC topper New Zealand, the Indian batters have to stay anchored. This is a line-up that no longer has Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Cheteshwar Pujara and Ajinkya Rahane. Gill and company get another opportunity to reiterate their credentials.

For some rugged inspiration they need not look beyond coach Gautam Gambhir in their dressing room. The doughty former India opener batted for 643 minutes while scoring a match-saving 137 in the Napier Test during the 2009 tour. The southpaw will be hoping that the current batting unit, which is high on flair, will remain sober and effectively counter the host. K.L. Rahul, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Devdutt Padikkal and Gill have the onerous task of negating the New Zealand seamers in their backyard. Rishabh Pant and Dhruv Jurel add depth, and if the former can successfully unleash his maverick batting approach, India can upset the host’s best-laid plans. New Zealand will miss the retired Kane Williamson but its batters would be comfortable on familiar surfaces. For India, much would hinge on how Jasprit Bumrah bowls. If the spearhead clicks, then it becomes easier for much of his support-cast that includes the persevering Mohammed Siraj, who was a touch rusty in Sri Lanka. From the squads of the past to the present unit, Ravindra Jadeja remains the link. Whether he will get a role to play or whether the management prefers an all-pace attack, remains a matter of conjecture. The home team led by Tom Latham will depend on Matt Henry, Kyle Jameson and other pacers, to choke the Indian batters. A hard task awaits India, first at Wellington and then at Christchurch.

fullParagraphs: A Division Bench said the State already had a large number of Tasmac shops, and considering the public interest, new Tasmac shops should not be opened
The Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court on Wednesday directed the State government not to open any new Tasmac liquor shops in Tamil Nadu.
A Division Bench of Justices P. Velmurugan and K.K. Ramakrishnan said the State already had a large number of Tasmac shops, and considering the public interest, new Tasmac shops should not be opened.
The court passed the direction while allowing a public interest litigation petition filed by V. Manikandan of Navakinathupatti in Nallampillai village in Tiruchi district.

The petitioner said about 30 families lived in the village, where agriculture was the predominant occupation. The authorities had proposed to establish a Tasmac shop at Navakinathupatti. He said school students pass through the proposed site to reach the government school at Karattupatti, and that the area was accident-prone.
The opening of a liquor shop in the area would affect the safety of women and the welfare of school students, he said. He pointed out that a Tasmac shop was already located in a nearby village.
He said there was no necessity or justification for establishing another liquor shop in the vicinity without assessing the existing outlet’s impact.

The residents had already requested the authorities not to establish any liquor shop in the village or in the surrounding villages, he said, seeking a direction to restrain the authorities from establishing the Tasmac shop.
The petitioner said he had made a detailed representation to the authorities concerned in this regard. However, no action had been taken so far.

articles.title: BJP turns to Mathura temple issue amid cadre unease, allies’ pressure
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Political observers say the renewed focus on Krishna Janmabhoomi serves as a “smokescreen” to mask simmering discontent among the party cadre over the UGC’s equity rules, SIR drive and seat sharing with alliance partners

Days after Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav made his ‘Dumdar Dalit’ outreach in Agra, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) responded on November 16 with ‘Radhe Radhe, Kamal Khila De’ and ‘Abki Baari Baanke Bihari’.

It was senior BJP leader and Deputy Chief Minister Keshav Prasad Maurya who spelt out to reporters, during the party’s two-day conclave in Mathura earlier this week, that constructing a grand temple at the Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi in Mathura would be at the centre of their campaign for the upcoming Uttar Pradesh Assembly election. The ruling party signalled that it would counter the SP’s ‘PDA’ [‘Pichhde’ (backward classes), Dalits and ‘Alpsankhyak’ (minorities)] card with the mantra of cultural nationalism, supplementing it with the ‘double-engine’ government’s “success stories” on the development and law and order fronts.

articles.title: India’s CSR spending leaves gaps in health, water security, innovation: Report
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), for instance, account for 60% of deaths in India, up from 45% in 2004-06. Yet, nearly 62% of identifiable NCD funding goes towards cancer, while cardiovascular diseases receive around 12%, despite accounting for over half of NCD deaths, says a study by a City-based global impact consulting firm

A significant share of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funding in India continues to flow towards established sectors, while several pressing development challenges receive comparatively limited attention, according to a report by Sattva Consulting and India Data Insights.
The analysis of CSR projects between FY23 and FY25 points to funding gaps in non-communicable diseases, women’s economic agency, school-to-work transition, groundwater resilience and innovation.

Nearly 80% of CSR funding is concentrated in five sectors, with education accounting for 35% and healthcare for 21%. However, the report finds gaps even within these established areas. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), for instance, account for 60% of deaths in India, up from 45% in 2004-06. Yet, nearly 62% of identifiable NCD funding goes towards cancer, while cardiovascular diseases receive around 12%, despite accounting for over half of the NCD deaths.

The report also points to a gap between education and employment outcomes. Youth unemployment stands at 9.9% rising to 25.9% among graduates. Of the CSR funding for the school-to-work transition, 42% goes towards academic and skilling support. For every rupee allocated to these areas, only 24 paise goes towards giving young people exposure to the world of work.

A similar concentration is visible in funding for women’s economic agency. The area receives ₹1,122.8 crore or 29% of identifiable women-focused CSR funding, with nearly 77% directed towards skilling and livelihoods. The report also highlights barriers such as inadequate care infrastructure, unsafe mobility and limited market access.

In groundwater resilience, Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana account for nearly 49% of India’s critical and over-exploited groundwater units, but receive only around 7% of identifiable CSR funding for the area.
Innovation and research also receive limited attention, with approximately ₹298 crore in CSR funding between FY23 and FY25. No industry directs more than 1.2% of its total CSR spending to this area.

“CSR has brought size and predictability to funding. It now needs agility. CSR cannot replace the government, but it can be patient and risk-tolerant in ways other capital often cannot. That allows it to test unproven models, build evidence on what works and help scale its adoption,” said Srikrishna Sridhar Murthy, co-founder and CEO of Sattva Consulting, a global impact consulting firm headquartered in Bengaluru.
“The question for corporates is no longer only how much they spend, but whether that spend is reaching the problems where it can make a difference,” Srikrishna added.
India’s annual CSR spending reached ₹40,794 crore in FY25, growing at 15% annually over the past decade.
