articles.title: Shiv Sena members tear pages of Sonia Gandhi’s book over Savarkar references, seek ban in Maharashtra
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The party has demanded that publisher HarperCollins withdraw two pages from the memoir, while the Congress condemned the protest and Uddhav Sena leaders hit back at the Shinde faction

Members of Shiv Sena on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) tore pages from Sonia Gandhi's memoir Belonging: A Journey of Love, demanding that the publisher withdraw two pages that the party claimed contained objectionable references to Vinayak Damodar Savarkar.

“We have torn the pages of the book as a mark of protest against the statements on Savarkar ji. We have sought that Harper Collins, the publisher, should scrap these two pages. Till they do that, we have sought that the Maharashtra government ban the sale of the book in the State. We will soon write to the government to seek a ban,” Shiv Sena leader Sanjay Nirupam told The Hindu .
He was among the six party spokespersons who addressed a press conference on Wednesday (November 18, 2026). The Shiv Sena is part of the ruling Mahayuti alliance in Maharashtra.

The Congress hit back at the Sena, condemning the act as “shameful”. “It shows intellectual bankruptcy. I feel pity for them. When you spit at the sun, the spit lands on you. It is a condemnable act,” Maharashtra Congress president Harshawardhan Sapkal said.

Former Chief Minister Prithviraj Chavan termed the act “childish”. “We are not the Taliban. We believe in the Constitution of Babasaheb Ambedkar. Everyone has the right to express their opinion. If you do not accept her views or if you think there are factual inaccuracies, refute them or point them out or write a separate book. But tearing a book is childishness,” he said.

Meanwhile, Shiv Sena leader Shaina NC tore a photograph bearing the image of Balasaheb Thackeray during the press conference. When this was pointed out to her, she was seen slipping the torn photograph under a pile of papers. She later justified the act, saying that the photograph showed Balasaheb Thackeray slapping an effigy of Manishankar Aiyar with a chappal.

“This is what he has taught us. We have only torn the pages of a book,” she said. She was later summoned by Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde. After the meeting, he said there was no question of anyone insulting Balasaheb Thackeray.
“He is venerable for us. Nobody can insult him,” Mr. Shinde said.

Meanwhile, the Uddhav Sena staged protests at several places in Maharashtra, including Mumbai. The issue also triggered a backlash in the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), where Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Kishori Pednekar engaged in a heated exchange with Mumbai Mayor Ritu Tawde.
The Shiv Sena said the references to Savarkar appeared on pages 201 and 443 of the book.

articles.title: Studies show trust in NDA government declining gradually, says Malcolm Adiseshiah awardee
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Raghav Gaiha, research affiliate, Population Aging Research Centre, University of Pennsylvania, and Kanika Mahajan, associate professor, Ashoka University, were presented the Malcolm Adiseshiah and Elizabeth Adiseshiah Awards, respectively

Recent economic studies in India point towards a gradual decline in trust on the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) government, according to Raghav Gaiha, research affiliate, Population Aging Research Centre, University of Pennsylvania, and former professor of public policy, Delhi University.

Delivering the Malcolm Adiseshiah Memorial Lecture on the topic ‘Subjective Well-Being, Trust, and Democracy in India’ at the Asian College of Journalism (ACJ) on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), Mr. Gaiha pointed out that erosion of public trust eroded the well-being of the people, threatening the very foundations of democracy. “Unless checked, continued erosion of trust, accumulated loss of well-being, and the brewing economic crisis together threaten to undermine the foundations of democracy,” he said.

Quoting political scientist P.K. Blind, he said trust in government represented confidence of citizens in the actions of a “government to do what was right and perceived fair”. Life evaluation, a measure of several components of well-being, including economic status, health, sense of security, family circumstances, and human and political rights, has perceptively deteriorated among people, he said quoting studies. Discrimination and violence against minorities, misleading claims of GDP growth in recent years, food price inflation and high unemployment, crackdown on the media, and denial of justice to certain sections have all contributed to the lowering of the subjective well-being, he added.

Delivering the Elizabeth Adiseshiah Memorial Lecture on the topic ‘Women and Work: The Missing Engine of India’s Development’, Kanika Mahajan, associate professor, Ashoka University, said India’s female labour force participation rate for women above 15 years stood at 32.8% in 2024 against a world average of 51% across 176 countries. “India sits among the lowest-ranked economies in the world on this measure, rivalled only by a few economies in West Asia and North Africa,” she added. While constraints at home, such as childcare, eldercare, safe transport, and availability of piped water, dictate women’s participation in economic activity, demand side constraints, such as quality of job creation for women, contribute to their participation as well, she said.
Mr. Gaiha was awarded the Malcolm Adiseshiah Award for his contribution to development studies and Ms. Mahajan was awarded the Elizabeth Adiseshiah Award.

C. Selvaraj, Chairman, Malcolm and Elizabeth Adiseshiah Trust, said the lectures pointed towards the multiplicity of quantifiable institutional factors that do not get into the reckoning of the quantitative economic reasoning, and those which economic models and quantitative measurements studiously avoid, he added.
Sashi Kumar, Chairman, ACJ, and A.R. Venkatachalapathy, professor, Madras Institute of Development Studies, also spoke.

articles.title: EPFO tells trustees there’s no legal route to recover ₹1,800 crore from Reliance Capital
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: EPFO’s Central Board of Trustees will discuss the status of the outstanding default on the retirement fund’s holdings and review the annual performance of its portfolio managers at a meeting on Thursday

The alleged siphoning of the remaining ₹1,800 crore of salaried workers’ money that Reliance Capital Ltd (RCL) has defaulted on paying to the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) is part of the agenda of the Central Board of Trustees (CBT) meeting, scheduled to be held here on Thursday (November 19, 2026). According to the agenda note, seen by The Hindu , the EPFO may not be able to claim any more of the principal amount or interest under any legal route.

Among the issues to be discussed in the meeting are the status of the outstanding default on the retirement fund’s holdings and the annual performance of its portfolio managers. CBT members will also discuss the material shared by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) on alleged fraudulent transactions, diversion of funds, irregular lending, and other alleged irregularities by the RCL.

The EPFO invested ₹2,500 crore of workers’ money with the RCL in 2013 and 2014, and the latter defaulted on it and is alleged to have impaired the security available to debenture holders, including the EPFO. The EPFO’s admitted claim from the RCL was ₹3,308.67 crore, out of which ₹2,500 crore was the principal amount invested. The investment was scheduled to mature in 2023 and 2024.

The custodian of the RCL, Standard Chartered Bank, has reported the receipt of ₹1,492.45 crore, i.e., 59.70% of the principal amount. “Total amount invested but not received as on 19.03.2025 is ₹1,007.55 crore, and the amount of interest admitted in Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) but not received is ₹808.67 crore,” the agenda note for Thursday’s meeting said.

The agenda note, citing the legal opinion of EPFO’s lawyer, added that no further legal remedy exists for additional recovery in view of binding Supreme Court judgments, the resolution plan approved by the National Company Law Tribunal, and the full-and-final settlement nature of distributions received. “The EPFO may not be able to claim further principal or interest under any legal route,” the agenda note adds.

A spokesperson for businessman Anil Ambani had earlier said that Mr. Ambani served as a non-executive director/chairman of the Board of Reliance Capital Limited from 2005 to November 2021, when the Reserve Bank of India superseded the board of directors of the company and appointed an administrator. “Mr. Ambani has denied any wrongdoing whatsoever and reserves all rights available to him in law,” the spokesperson had said.

The EPFO has told its trustees that the Central Bureau of Investigation has registered a case into the matter. The organisation has written to the ED on the issue and asked the Ministry of Corporate Affairs to refer the matter to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO).

“Considering the nature of the allegations and the financial loss suffered by EPFO, legal consultation was sought on the matter. Based on the legal opinion received, a reference was made to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) for registration of FIR, investigation into the alleged fraudulent transactions, and for such appropriate action in accordance with the law,” says the agenda note circulated among members.

The meeting will also discuss the status of other defaulters, including the Uttar Pradesh Financial Corporation (outstanding interest of about ₹85 crore), Richardson & Cruddas (a penal interest of about ₹5.36 crore), Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Limited (a claim of ₹601.54 crore), and the Punjab State Industrial Development Corporation (₹1.10 crore interest in default).

The meeting will also review the performance of portfolio managers such as the UTI Asset Management Company Ltd, SBI Fund Management Ltd, and four asset management companies for Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF) investments — UTI Asset Management Company Limited, SBI Funds Management Limited, ICICI Prudential Asset Management Company Limited, and Nippon India Life AMC. The evaluation report is prepared by M/s. CRISIL.

articles.title: India imposes 162.5% duty and tax on bulk Scotch imports amid UK trade pact dispute
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: More than 80 containers belonging to Pernod Ricard, Diageo and Bacardi remain stuck at Indian ports as the dispute over customs classification threatens to disrupt the liquor industry.

India is imposing an effective duty of 162.5% on bulk Scotch imports amid an ongoing dispute over the India-UK trade agreement, raising concerns among liquor companies as the levy exceeds the 150% charged before the agreement, according to eight sources and a government document.

The India-UK trade agreement, implemented in July, halved tariffs on Scotch to 75%. Businesses and the British government had hailed the move as a major win for companies such as Pernod Ricard and Diageo, which import Scotch in bulk and blend it to make popular products for India’s USD 65-billion liquor market.

However, in the first major dispute linked to the trade agreement, Indian investigators have argued that companies are using incorrect customs classifications for bulk Scotch concentrates, which are treated as raw materials used to make drinks such as blended whiskies.

Since May, such imports have been classified under a newly created customs category for “compound alcoholic preparations”, which attracts a 150% t tariff, according to Indian investigators. These imports are then subject to a consumption tax, taking the total duty to 162.5% , according to a government document reviewed by Reuters and eight sources, including industry executives and customs agents familiar with the matter.
As the dispute continues, thousands of litres of bulk Scotch in more than 80 shipping containers belonging to Pernod, Diageo and Bacardi remain stuck at ports, Reuters reported last week.
Under a provisional release arrangement pending investigation, 75% of the goods’ value must be paid upfront, with the remaining amount covered by bank guarantees, the sources said.

“Industry has already reduced prices of Scotch products in the market when the India-UK pact kicked in, and now they are faced with higher duties again,” said a source in the liquor importing business.
Pernod, which owns UK-based Chivas Brothers, Diageo and several other Indian companies believe that both bulk and bottled Scotch imports should be taxed at 75% under the trade agreement.
The British government has repeatedly said in statements that it is working with New Delhi to resolve the issue, while India has said the dispute will be settled soon.

Pernod and Diageo have moved to arrange bank guarantees and other funding to secure the release of their blocked containers and ensure business continuity. Bacardi is still deciding its next steps, three of the sources said.

articles.title: UN Sustainable Development Goals group for science, technology rejigged
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The group has been constituted even as the international community ramps up efforts to achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development

The United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has reconstituted a 10-member group that works on promoting science, technology and innovation toward achieving its Sustainable Development Goals. The lone Indian in this group is former biologist and former Council of Scientific and Industrial Research CSIR Director General, Shekhar Mande, who is also currently President, Indian National Science Academy.
The group has been constituted even as the international community ramps up efforts to achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, while preparing for the 2027 SDG Summit.

“The group comprises distinguished experts from diverse geographic and disciplinary backgrounds from both developing and developed countries. Each member, recognised for their international excellence in science or technology, brings a wealth of experience and insight from civil society, the private sector, and the scientific community, underscoring the inclusive and comprehensive approach the UN is taking towards sustainable development,” an accompanying press statement noted.

The other members of the group are Marian Dorcas Quain (Ghana), Deputy Director-General of CSIR Ghana; Giorgio Rossi (Italy), Vice-President of Elettra-Sincrotrone Trieste; Magnus Andersson (Sweden), Associate Professor at Malmö University; Mônica Tejo Cavalcanti (Brazil), Professor at the Federal University of Campina Grande; Evgeniya Dmitrieva (Russia), Member of the Civic Chamber of the Russian Federation; Motoko Kotani (Japan), Executive Director of Science at RIKEN; Jin Li (China), President of Fudan University; Madin Maseeh (Maldives), President of the Maldives Space Research Organisation; and Rita Orji (Nigeria), Canada Research Chair in Persuasive Technology at Dalhousie University.
Professor Mande is also President of Vijnana Bharti, which, along with the Ministry of Science and Technology is gearing up to host the India International Science Festival in Pune in December.

Announcing this on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), Union Minister of Science Jitendra Singh said at a press briefing that the government had taken a conscious decision to replace “scattered, repetitive gatherings”, including the erstwhile Indian Science Congress, with two flagship national events carrying distinct identities.

While the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave in October saw 13 Ministries and Nobel Laureates, and was an academic-driven conclave exploring frontier themes, the India International Science Festival (IISF) brought a “festive, public-facing character with international resonance”. By rotating the venue to different regions, after Chandigarh, Hyderabad, Goa and Delhi, bringing IISF for the first time to Pune leverages the western hub’s vibrant academic, research, and industrial ecosystem.

articles.title: Bangladesh deploys paramilitary as unrest grows over Hasina's return
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles ​being torched in at least ‌28 districts over the last 10 days, with several police personnel and civilians injured, local media has reported

Bangladesh ‌stepped up security and deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops nationwide on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) ​as the planned return of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has ⁠sparked clashes, bomb blasts, and arson attacks blamed on supporters of her banned party.

Ms. Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent protests demanding ‌her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card, saying she plans to return in December.
But the government ‌has so far rejected her request, leading to members and supporters of ‌her ⁠Awami League party taking to the streets in protest.
Last week, the party ⁠announced a week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support for Ms. Hasina's return, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on November 19.

Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles ​being torched in at least ‌28 districts over the last 10 days, with several police personnel and civilians injured, local media has reported.

Late on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest ‌near Ms. Hasina's home district of Gopalganj, police said.

On the same night, a ​crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and ⁠shops belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday (November 18, 2026) morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district ‌of Pirojpur after two buses were set on fire, authorities said.

Tuesday (November 17, 2026) marked the day on which Ms. Hasina was sentenced to death a year ago by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on the student-led uprising against her in 2024.

At least 37 Grameen Bank branches and offices have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires ‌since November 10, with 14 more attacked since midnight on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), the bank said.

articles.title: Brace for impact: On rising inflation and external factors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: High inflation due to external factors could soon exacerbate economic pain

India’s much-hyped domestic economic resilience is set to be tested over the next few months as external factors start to impose inescapable pressures. A case in point is inflation. The latest data on retail inflation show that it crossed the Reserve Bank of India’s 6% upper comfort limit in October 2026. According to economists, this is likely to continue through the third quarter of this financial year, which means at least two more months of high inflation. Agricultural shortfalls brought on by a patchy and deficient monsoon have meant that food inflation rose sharply to 8.5% in October 2026. Elevated fuel prices meant that inflation in the transport category also rose sharply. What is worse is that high inflation is spreading to almost every aspect of a household’s day-to-day needs. In fact, the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) data show that 10 of the 12 major categories saw inflation in October, hitting their highest levels recorded in the new series of the index. So, things such as clothing, footwear, housing, furnishings, and services such as healthcare, education, communication, recreation, and restaurant and hospitality are not only getting more expensive, but they are doing so at an accelerating rate. This would have been bad enough had wages been increasing in real terms. Yet, the latest research by Data for India on the country’s official wage statistics shows that, while nominal wages doubled from 2012 to 2024, they actually fell 4% over the same period after adjusting for inflation. And this is sharper for high-skilled and high-earning workers. Lower wage earners saw marginal increases over this period. While this is of some comfort, it is the higher wage earners that drive consumption in an economy. Real wage contraction for them, which is likely to have worsened in 2026, will hit consumption levels and private investment.

Further, there is strong evidence to suggest that the official inflation metrics are not capturing the full extent of rising prices. Data on cash with the public and UPI transactions show the value of both has been growing in double digits over the last year and more, significantly outpacing nominal GDP growth. This either suggests that the informal economy is far larger than earlier thought or, more likely, that inflation is well above what the official figures are being able to capture. Unfortunately, there are no real magic-wand fixes to this situation. Inflation is largely beyond the government’s control, and wage growth cannot happen overnight. The only way forward is to continue trying to spur sector-specific growth and warn people of the impending storm.

articles.title: Critical ban: On recycling of lithium-ion batteries
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India needs to create an entire ecosystem for recycling of lithium-ion batteries

On November 10, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass by moving it from the “free” to the “prohibited” list of exports. Black mass is an intermediate product when spent batteries and factory scrap are shredded. It contains valuable lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite. The Commerce Ministry says the ban will ensure feedstock for domestic refiners, lift their capacity utilisation and draw investment. While the recycling of lead-acid batteries end-to-end is an established ecosystem and formalised, too, lithium-ion battery recycling is an emerging segment with only a few dozen licensed operators but has much potential given the scale of use of such batteries in EVs. While the ban will redirect supply, it will not automatically create a market and ecosystem. Just banning export without creating an entire ecosystem will only lead to dumping of lithium-ion batteries into landfills if the blackmass has no market. Blackmass production is a largely mechanical process but further downstream processing is more specialised chemical processing requiring larger investment and further policy support. If downstream units are online, their output can directly feed into indigenous lithium-ion battery manufacture.

India depends heavily on imports for critical minerals such as those used in battery inputs. Beyond working on supply aspects, the government must address the price gap to create a robust recycling market. Under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, producers buy extended producer responsibility (EPR) certificates from recyclers but these are undervalued. Cheap certificates reward recycling on paper over investment in high-yield plants. A floor price that covers the full cost of recovery, with digital tracking, would fix that. Rare earths show how recycling remains a missed opportunity for India because of policy gaps. A smartphone can be up to 1% neodymium-iron-boron magnet by weight. That puts its rare earth content at about 3,000 parts per million, comparable to India’s monazite beach sands. Extracting it takes less energy than mining. A magnet separated from the phone is about 30% rare earth. Magnets make up as much as 3% of a hard drive, but are usable only if they are removed before the drive is shredded for data destruction. Yet the e-waste rules do not require rare earth separation. Rare earths need a separate EPR category, too. Payment by weight cannot be applied for rare earth minerals.

✍️ Editorial & Opinion 📅 17 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 3 Min Read

📰 Critical ban: On recycling of lithium-ion batteries

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

India needs to create an entire ecosystem for recycling of lithium-ion batteries

On November 10, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass by moving it from the “free” to the “prohibited” list of exports. Black mass is an intermediate product when spent batteries and factory scrap are shredded. It contains valuable lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite. The Commerce Ministry says the ban will ensure feedstock for domestic refiners, lift their capacity utilisation and draw investment. While the recycling of lead-acid batteries end-to-end is an established ecosystem and formalised, too, lithium-ion battery recycling is an emerging segment with only a few dozen licensed operators but has much potential given the scale of use of such batteries in EVs. While the ban will redirect supply, it will not automatically create a market and ecosystem. Just banning export without creating an entire ecosystem will only lead to dumping of lithium-ion batteries into landfills if the blackmass has no market. Blackmass production is a largely mechanical process but further downstream processing is more specialised chemical processing requiring larger investment and further policy support. If downstream units are online, their output can directly feed into indigenous lithium-ion battery manufacture.

India depends heavily on imports for critical minerals such as those used in battery inputs. Beyond working on supply aspects, the government must address the price gap to create a robust recycling market. Under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, producers buy extended producer responsibility (EPR) certificates from recyclers but these are undervalued. Cheap certificates reward recycling on paper over investment in high-yield plants. A floor price that covers the full cost of recovery, with digital tracking, would fix that. Rare earths show how recycling remains a missed opportunity for India because of policy gaps. A smartphone can be up to 1% neodymium-iron-boron magnet by weight. That puts its rare earth content at about 3,000 parts per million, comparable to India’s monazite beach sands. Extracting it takes less energy than mining. A magnet separated from the phone is about 30% rare earth. Magnets make up as much as 3% of a hard drive, but are usable only if they are removed before the drive is shredded for data destruction. Yet the e-waste rules do not require rare earth separation. Rare earths need a separate EPR category, too. Payment by weight cannot be applied for rare earth minerals.

articles.title: In a dilemma: On Sheikh Hasina and India-Bangladesh ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India must improve ties with Bangladesh, and protect Hasina

Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina now in exile in India, has set off speculation about her imminent return to Dhaka by submitting an application for a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card this week. The application, made through the Bangladesh High Commission in Delhi, was dismissed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir, who said that the government in Dhaka would not grant a passport to a “terrorist”, and would seek her return via the extradition agreement as a “prisoner transfer process” with India. Ms. Hasina has already announced that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December this year, as she did after her previous stay in India in exile from 1975-1981, after the brutal assassination of her father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and nearly every other member of her family. However, the situation is considerably different now. This time, Ms. Hasina came to India in 2024 fleeing mobs of protestors that overthrew her government, and has since been convicted by a tribunal for ordering a crackdown on thousands of students, and sentenced to death. In interviews, including to The Hindu , Ms. Hasina says she hopes to return to Bangladesh to argue her case and rebuild her party, the Awami League, but that is hardly likely, given the anger against her amongst the polity, and bipartisan consensus to ban the Awami League from politics. Despite the harsh rhetoric it employs against her, the BNP government is unlikely to wish for her return, as it would have to begin execution proceedings against the 79-year-old former Prime Minister, with international opposition to such a move expected to be voluble. Not doing so would only strengthen its opposition party, the Jamaat-e-Islami, that has accused the Rahman government of soft-pedalling the issue. The government must also worry about possible protests and violence within the country in the event Ms. Hasina returns.

The situation puts the Modi government in a spot. Ever since Ms. Hasina announced plans to return, during a virtual press conference held in Delhi on August 5 this year, Delhi-Dhaka ties have been on a downslide. The government’s decision not to prevent Ms. Hasina from addressing the press, where she used the opportunity to soundly criticise PM Rahman, meant the abrupt cancellation of the Bangladesh PM’s visit. Next month, the Indo-Bangladesh Ganga Water treaty is set to expire, and talks on its extension have also become a casualty. Ms. Hasina has been an honoured guest in India, and the government cannot physically restrain her from taking the flight to Dhaka or travelling to the land border at Petrapole to cross over. Nor can it wash its hands of her situation once she crosses over. New Delhi must redouble its diplomatic efforts on improving bilateral ties while also ensuring Ms. Hasina’s welfare.

Editorial Context: In a dilemma: On Sheikh Hasina and India-Bangladesh ties. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

articles.title: MLAs cannot threaten government officials and browbeat them into submission: Madras High Court
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Justice V. Lakshminarayanan dismisses a plea by DMK former MLA C.M.P. Ezhilarasan to quash a case booked against him for threatening Kancheepuram Collector’s personal assistant

A Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) cannot threaten government officials and browbeat them into submission for such threats, apart from being unconstitutional, it would amount to preventing the officers from performing their official duties, the Madras High Court observed on Monday (November 16, 2026).

Justice V. Lakshminarayanan wrote: “If the Revenue department officials cannot threaten an MLA, similarly an MLA too cannot threaten the officials and browbeat them into submission.” He made the observation while dismissing a petition filed by DMK former MLA C.V.M.P. Ezhilarasan to quash a criminal case pending against him.

The Kanchi Taluk police had registered a First Information Report (FIR) against the petitioner for having abused, in filthy language, and threatened the Personal Assistant (General) to the Kancheepuram Collector because he was miffed over distribution of tokens for the Athi Varadar festival at the Devarajaswamy Temple in 2019.

According to the complainant A. Kumaran, the petitioner, who was the then MLA of the constituency, had barged into the Collector’s camp office on August 5, 2019 and asked where the Collector was. On being told that the Collector was in a meeting, he used a filthy word to abuse the officials and attempted to assault the complainant.

The complainant also claimed that the petitioner had threatened to finish him off before walking out of the camp office and indulging in a road blockade along with his supporters. Since the trial in the case was slated to begin shortly, the petitioner had rushed to the High Court with a plea to quash the charge sheet.

Refusing to quash the criminal proceedings, Justice Lakshminarayanan said, the role of an MLA was inside the Legislative Assembly and it could not extend to the level of holding out threats to government officials. The judge also appreciated the complainant for showing courage to stand up against the legislator and the other eye witnesses for supporting him.

The judge, however, sounded a word of caution that all observations made by him were on the basis of prima facie materials and limited to the purpose of dismissing the quash petition. He said, the veracity of the allegations levelled against the petitioner could be decided only after the conduct of a full fledged trial and appreciation of evidence.

articles.title: Paharganj building collapse: Two held, MCD says no construction work was underway amid GRAP restrictions
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Delhi Police held the owner and contractor of an under-construction hotel in Paharganj after a building collapse injured eight workers. The MCD said no construction work was underway at the time of the incident despite GRAP restrictions.

The Delhi police on Monday (November 16) arrested the owner and contractor of an under-construction hotel in Paharganj and registered an FIR against them, a day after a portion of the building collapsed, injuring eight workers.
“The property owner Raman and a contractor Anwar have been apprehended and are being bound down,” Deputy Commissioner of Police (Central) Rohit Rajbir Singh said.

The accused, identified as property owner Raman and contractor Anwar, were booked under Sections 290 (negligent conduct with respect to buildings), 125(a) (act endangering life or personal safety), 223(a) (disobedience of an order duly promulgated by a public servant) and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, added Mr. Singh.

The incident occurred amid restrictions on dust-generating outdoor construction activities imposed to curb air pollution under the Graded Response Action Plan. However, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) maintained that construction was not underway at the time of the incident.

articles.title: Plea in SC says ghost Form 7s haunt Mustafabad constituency during Delhi SIR
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The petition said persons declared dead were alive, while persons said to have shifted were found at home. Thirty-seven applications examined by the authorities were found to be false or fabricated.

Congress leader Ali Mehdi approached the Supreme Court on Monday alleging that Assembly Constituency-69 (AC-69) of Mustafabad is seeing a “substantial” amount of ghost Form 7s seeking deletion of voters in the ongoing Delhi SIR, and a crisis of electoral integrity is brewing.

The writ petition filed through advocate Shariq Ahmed, and highlighting multiple reports by The Hindu, said voters whose names feature for deletion on the grounds of death, absence and permanent shifting were found to be very much alive, present and staying put at their recorded addresses on the electoral roll.

The persons in whose names Form 7s have been filed for deletion of these voters deny having filed or signed on the applications. The petition alleged that ghost Form 7s seemed to have been filed by phantom objectors in the Mustafabad constituency.

“The integrity of an electoral roll is compromised not only when an ineligible name remains upon it. It is equally compromised when an eligible elector is removed from it on a fact which never existed or upon an objection which the supposed objector never made. The present record discloses the latter danger in its stark form,” the writ petition said.
It said persons declared dead were alive, while persons said to have shifted were found at home. Thirty-seven applications examined by the authorities were found to be false or fabricated.
“The existence of a genuine objector and the existence of a genuine ground for deletion — In Mustafabad, both are under serious doubt at the same time,” Mr. Ahmed submitted.

Section 22 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 requires the Electoral Registration Officer to be satisfied, after proper verification of the facts, before an entry can be corrected or deleted.

Rule 13(2) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 requires an objection to the proposed inclusion of a name or an application for deletion to be made in Form 7 and to be preferred by a person whose own name is included in the electoral roll.
Form 7 requires identification of the applicant, identification of the elector objected to, the particular ground for deletion and a declaration as to the truth of the particulars stated.
The guidelines accompanying the form place the onus of substantiating the ground upon the applicant.

articles.title: India's exports up 29.9% in October; trade deficit narrows to $20.09 billion
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The growth in India’s merchandise exports in October, the fastest in five years and faster than import growth, indicates that volumes of exports are growing along with prices
India’s merchandise exports rose to an all-time high of $49.5 billion in October 2026, bringing down the country’s overall trade deficit, official data released on Friday showed.
While a large part of this growth was due to petroleum products, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said diversification of exports to various locations helped improve the numbers.
India’s total exports, including goods and services, stood at $89.99 billion in October 2026, up nearly 30% from last October.
The overall trade deficit shrank from $25.1 billion last October to $20.1 billion year-on-year.

“In the month of October, the exports of merchandise exports have registered a new peak of $49.47 billion,” Mr. Agrawal said at a press briefing. “This is the highest-ever monthly merchandise export value, along with the highest monthly growth of 45.03% in the last five years.”
Merchandise imports rose to a record high of $89.35 billion in October 2026, up 16.5% YoY. Total imports stood at $110.1 billion, a 16.6% increase.

According to trade experts, goods exports growing faster than merchandise imports shows that while the rise in global prices contributed to the increase in the value of India’s exports, there was also an increase in the underlying export volumes.

“The particularly encouraging part of this growth is that this is not in any particular sector, this is not in any particular geography, it is broad-based across countries and regions,” Mr. Agrawal added. “43 of our 50 top export destinations posted positive growth in October 2026 as compared to 2025.”
The data show that India’s exports to 12 out of its top 20 export destinations grew by double digits or more.
Mr. Agrawal pointed out that India’s exports to its free trade agreement (FTA) partners had grown strongly.

India’s official position since the Pahalgam attack and the ensuing confrontations along the border is that terrorism and bilateral talks cannot coexist. articles.title: Outlook outage: On Microsoft and dangers of centralising digital systems
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The dangers of centralising the internet’s architecture are now clear

Last week, Microsoft’s suite of productivity and email software, which businesses, governments, hospitals and a host of other organisations rely upon round-the-clock, abruptly stopped working globally , affecting tens of millions of people around the world. The company has cited a network upgrade gone awry as the root cause of the incident. Incidents such as the Microsoft 365 outage are a natural consequence of businesses and governments allowing key digital systems to become centralised all over the world. The internet remains, and was pioneered as, a network of networks. If one business’s networks went down, the reasoning went, others would not fall like dominos: everyone was, after all, connected to everyone else. But the economics have long been prohibitive, with dedicated servers and web-connected infrastructure infeasible for all but the largest businesses, with even those firms seeking the enticing cost savings from socialised infrastructure. That made sense: the internet made shared infrastructure more economical, allowing hardware and maintenance costs to be spread so far and wide that at a per-user level prices have been negligible. Competition among major cloud providers, the few that remain at Microsoft’s scale, have kept prices affordable for enterprise software for all shades of organisations.

Digital services have grown more sophisticated, and more deeply integrated into the economy as this centralisation unfolded. But the downside is that, regardless of the sophistication and professionalism of any company, mistakes happen, and the scale of these mistakes can quickly cascade over to the entire economy. There are societal and organisational lessons to be gleaned from these episodes. There is no such thing as a reliable vendor. Governments must also draw a cyber sovereignty lesson here that does not simply entail swapping a global vendor for a domestic one. It is the subversion of the internet’s architecture that is at the root of these incidents. Investing in resilience — and shielding critical operations from destabilising disruptions, no matter how improbable — should inform attitudes to digital systems. As a new generation of AI data centres is poised to supercharge the centralised systems of yesteryear, it is all the more imperative to mitigate even occasional vagaries of large systems.

articles.title: Kerala High Court refers petition challenging clean chit to Chief Minister in Punarjani case to Chief Justice
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: High Court Registry directed to place the matter before the Chief Justice to decide whether the case would be considered by the court trying MP/MLA cases, Prevention of Corruption Act, or as a PIL

A Single Bench of the Kerala High Court has referred the petition challenging the closure of the preliminary inquiry against Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan in the Punarjani case for consideration before the appropriate court.

Justice C. Jayachandran observed that there was a strong prima facie indication that the petition had features of a public interest litigation (PIL). The Bench directed the High Court Registry to place the matter before the Chief Justice to decide whether the case would be considered by the court trying MP/MLA cases, Prevention of Corruption Act, or as a PIL.

The petition had been filed by lawyer K.M. Shajahan challenging a Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) report closing the preliminary inquiry and dropping corruption charges against the Chief Minister in connection with the Punarjani flood rehabilitation scheme.

The court examined two aspects while considering the petition — first, if the petitioner had the right to challenge the preliminary inquiry report, and second, if the court had the jurisdiction to hear the matter.

The petitioner argued that he had preferred the plea in his capacity as a citizen and a whistleblower, with every right to challenge the report. The State pointed out that a petition in this regard was filed by one of the complainants in the Punarjani case. This petition was later withdrawn and filed as a PIL seeking a CBI probe. However, the PIL was dismissed by a Division Bench of the court. The State contended that the petitioner did not have any right to move the petition since the complaint had already been decided by the court.
The Single Bench found that the jurisdiction to try the case would have to be decided first before examining the rights of the petitioner.

articles.title: Delhi’s construction boom, workers’ growing risks: Safety takes a back seat as violations go unchecked
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Missing helmets and protective gear, unsafe structures, punishing work hours and rushed construction expose a deepening safety crisis at Delhi’s building sites, where basic safeguards are routinely ignored and accountability often comes only after tragedy strikes

A day after an under-construction hotel building collapsed in Delhi’s Paharganj, leaving eight workers injured, the Delhi Police apprehended the property owner and contractor on Monday (November 16, 2026), bringing the spotlight back on rampant safety violations at construction sites across the Capital.

The two accused, identified as Raman and Anwar, were booked under Sections 290 (negligent conduct with respect to buildings), 125(a) (act endangering life or personal safety), 223(a) (disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant) and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), according to DCP (Central) Rohit Rajbir Singh.
The construction was also underway despite a ban on outdoor construction imposed as part of measures to curb air pollution, making it only one of the violations among many others.
The property owner, Raman (left), and contractor Anwar (right) of the building that collapsed in Central Delhi’s Paharganj, injuring 8 people on November 15 | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement
The incident came just 10 days after seven workers were killed when an “unauthorised” three-storey building under construction collapsed in Old Delhi’s Chawri Bazar .
The recurring incidents have exposed a pattern of unsafe construction, inadequate safeguards and weak enforcement, with violations coming into focus only after a collapse claims lives.

But for the workers who build the city, unsafe conditions are not confined to the moments when a structure gives way. Missing helmets, inadequate protective equipment, long working hours and contractors racing against deadlines are part of their everyday working conditions, they told The Hindu.

“Basic safety equipment, including industrial shoes, gloves, uniforms and good-quality helmets, is not provided by contractors. They simply tell us, ‘Jo hai bas aajao ’ [come with whatever you have],” said Raja, a construction worker from Mandawali who was also at the Chawri Bazar site on November 5.
The safety gear, he said, is sometimes brought out only when an inspection or an official visit is expected. Workers are asked to wear uniforms that otherwise remain unavailable to them.

Buildings with four or five storeys are now being put up in as little as 20-25 days, he said, with contractors assigning work in the morning and expecting it to be completed by the end of the day. “We work at least 12 hours a day with only half a day off on Sundays to earn around ₹17,000-18,000 a month. We don’t know what will happen at work which will claim our lives,” he said.

articles.title: Committee to inspect Valagerahalli Lake
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: It directs BWSSB, civic body to stop sewage inflow, clear waste and take up lake rejuvenation
The Lokayukta has acted on a petition filed by local residents, who raised concerns over the deteriorating condition of Valagerahalli Lake and the health hazards it poses.

After examining the complaints and a report submitted by the executive engineer of the lake division of the Bengaluru West City Corporation, the Lokayukta observed that sewage was entering the lake along with rainwater. The Lokayukta expressed concern over the lack of adequate action by the authorities to prevent pollution and protect the lake.

A joint inspection committee comprising the Chief Engineer (TAC) of the Karnataka Lokayukta, Superintendent of Police-1, Karnataka Lokayukta, and officials of the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board has been constituted. The committee has been directed to inspect the lake, assess its present condition, and submit a report with recommendations by November 30.
The Lokayukta said action would be initiated against officials found guilty of dereliction of duty if steps were not taken to resolve the issue.

1. Core Context & Background: It directs BWSSB, civic body to stop sewage inflow, clear waste and take up lake rejuvenation

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: The Lokayukta said action would be initiated against officials found guilty of dereliction of duty if steps were not taken to resolve the issue.

articles.title: A poverty line that falls short
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Reliable poverty estimates are not just for academic purposes. India has made real progress, but without a credible benchmark, it is hard to say how much, or how much remains to be done

There is no serious doubt that poverty in India has fallen sharply over the past decade. However, researchers and policymakers cannot agree on how many are still poor. Depending on the estimate, the share ranges from about 5% to more than 26%. Take the recent World Bank report. At its international line of $3 a day (2021 PPP), 2.6% of Indians were poor in 2022-23. Raise the line to $4.20, the bank’s benchmark for lower middle-income countries, and the figure jumps to around 16.1%. Same country, same year. Only the yardstick changed. A low level of extreme poverty does not necessarily mean poverty is not still a major issue. Where you draw the line decides how much economic insecurity you see.

India’s own figures tell a similar convoluted story. For example, SBI Research (2025) takes the Tendulkar line of 2009, adjusts it for inflation, and gets poverty of 7.2% in rural India and 4.6% in urban India for 2022-23. Rangarajan and Dev (2014), using an inflation-adjusted version of the Rangarajan Committee line, arrive at 10.8%. Further, Sethu, Surya and Ruthu (2024), who rebuild the Rangarajan method from the latest consumption survey, report 26.4%. Most of that gap boils down to the lines themselves: SBI’s Tendulkar-based lines use, after adjusting for inflation, about ₹1,632 a month per person in rural areas and ₹1,944 in urban areas. In contrast, Sethu et al. use much higher thresholds of ₹2,515 and ₹3,639. And the outcomes are obvious: Higher lines, higher poverty. Method matters too. One camp takes an old line and adjusts it for inflation. The other reconstructs the line from spending patterns in the new survey. Both have limitations, and they are answering different questions.
Macroeconomic & Financial Update: A poverty line that falls short. This development reflects key trends in India's fiscal roadmap, monetary policy transmission, and banking sector resilience.

articles.summary: Reliable poverty estimates are not just for academic purposes. India has made real progress, but without a credible benchmark, it is hard to say how much, or how much remains to be done
articles.keyPoints:
• Reliable poverty estimates are not just for academic purposes. India has made real progress, but without a credible benchmark, it is hard to say how much, or how much remains to be done
• There is no serious doubt that poverty in India has fallen sharply over the past decade. However, researchers and policymakers cannot agree on how many are still poor. Depending on the estimate, the share ranges from about 5% to more than 26%. Take the recent World Bank report. At its international line of $3 a day (2021 PPP), 2.6% of Indians were poor in 2022-23. Raise the line to $4.20, the bank’s benchmark for lower middle-income countries, and the figure jumps to around 16.1%. Same country, same year. Only the yardstick changed. A low level of extreme poverty does not necessarily mean poverty is not still a major issue. Where you draw the line decides how much economic insecurity you see.
• India’s own figures tell a similar convoluted story. For example, SBI Research (2025) takes the Tendulkar line of 2009, adjusts it for inflation, and gets poverty of 7.2% in rural India and 4.6% in urban India for 2022-23. Rangarajan and Dev (2014), using an inflation-adjusted version of the Rangarajan Committee line, arrive at 10.8%. Further, Sethu, Surya and Ruthu (2024), who rebuild the Rangarajan method from the latest consumption survey, report 26.4%. Most of that gap boils down to the lines themselves: SBI’s Tendulkar-based lines use, after adjusting for inflation, about ₹1,632 a month per person in rural areas and ₹1,944 in urban areas. In contrast, Sethu et al. use much higher thresholds of ₹2,515 and ₹3,639. And the outcomes are obvious: Higher lines, higher poverty. Method matters too. One camp takes an old line and adjusts it for inflation. The other reconstructs the line from spending patterns in the new survey. Both have limitations, and they are answering different questions.

articles.title: No proof from ECI to show SIR was a ‘unanimous’ decision, Rahul Gandhi to Supreme Court
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The ECI’s October 26 affidavit, in response to a petition filed by INDIA bloc leaders led by Mr. Gandhi, denied any differences of opinion between the CEC and the Election Commissioners over the SIR process

Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi told the Supreme Court on Monday (November 16, 2026) that the Election Commission of India (ECI) failed to produce any proof to establish its claim that the special intensive revision (SIR) was a “unanimous” decision made by Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar , and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.

“No minutes of the meeting, file notings, recorded approvals, agenda, deliberations or other primary material evidencing the participation and approval of all three members have been produced with the ECI counter-affidavit of October 26,” Mr. Gandhi submitted in his rejoinder.

Mr. Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders have also separately filed an application containing a set of “interrogatories” directed at the CEC, the two Election Commissioners, and other senior ECI officials involved in the SIR. The pointed questions inquire about the number and details of each SIR file, as well as the specific occasions between February 19, 2025, and October 26, 2026, on which the two Election Commissioners objected in writing or expressed dissent or reservation regarding any matter related to the SIR, ECINET, Form 6, or the filing of appeals.
The case is scheduled for hearing on November 17 before a Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant.

The reported friction between Mr. Kumar and the two Election Commissioners over the SIR and the CEC’s allegedly unilateral and authoritarian conduct, had triggered widespread protests across India demanding his removal from office.

The ECI’s October 26 affidavit, in response to a petition filed by INDIA bloc leaders led by Mr. Gandhi, denied any differences of opinion between the CEC and the Election Commissioners over the SIR process.

Mr. Gandhi said the court must not accept such “bare assertions” from the ECI. He questioned why the affidavit was filed by the ECI when Mr. Kumar, Mr. Sandhu and Mr. Joshi were separately made respondents.
The Opposition leader, represented by senior advocate A.M. Singhvi and advocate Prasanna S., said the EC chose not to explain when and where exactly the decision to conduct a nationwide SIR was made.

The ECI affidavit’s blank assertions contradict its own Right to Information (RTI) response that “the Commission has so far not taken any decision on initiating a special intensive revision (SIR) across the country in 2025”.

Mr. Gandhi said the ECI’s claim of a “unanimous” Commission did not quite agree with the fact that Mr. Sandhu and Mr. Joshi took the unprecedented step of writing directly to the Cabinet Secretary, conveying their displeasure over the conduct of affairs within the poll body during the SIR exercise.

articles.title: Bilkis Bano case: Supreme Court suspends sentence, grants bail to two convicts
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The order published on the court website reasoned that the two men had already been imprisoned for more than 17 years and one of them suffers a severe handicap
The Supreme Court has granted bail to two convicts undergoing life imprisonment for the gangrape of Bilkis Bano and the murder of her family, including a two-month-old infant, during the 2002 riots.
Justices M. M. Sundresh and Prasanna B. Varale suspended the life sentences of Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya on October 28.

The short order, published recently on the court website, reasoned that the two men had already been imprisoned for more than 17 years and one of them suffers a severe handicap. Besides, the court said there were “issues to be decided in the appeal, both on fact and law”.

Senior advocate Siddharth Luthra, for the appellants, argued that Modhiya had not been named in the FIR, and was only implicated in the crime after a substantial period of nearly three years. Joshi, who underwent leg surgery, was described as handicapped.

"Additional Solicitor General Raja Thakre and counsels for Gujarat and Maharashtra, Swati Ghildayal and Aaditya Aniruddha Pande, objected to the plea for bail and suspension of sentence. They argued that the offence was very serious, and their conviction by the trial court was confirmed in the High Court.

“Having heard the parties, it suffices to state that the appellants have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years, and also the fact remains that one of the appellants has a severe handicap. Certainly, there are issues to be decided in the appeal, both on fact and law. In view of the above and considering the issues involved in this appeal, we suspend the sentence and grant bail to the appellants on such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the trial court,” the Bench ordered.

The interim order was passed in an appeal filed by the two men against a May 2017 judgment of the Bombay High Court upholding their life sentences. A CBI Special Judge in Greater Mumbai had convicted the 11 men and sentenced them to life imprisonment in January 2008.
In 2024, the apex court quashed the order of en masse remission granted by the State of Gujarat in August 2022 to the 11 men.

The case was transferred by the Supreme Court in August 2004 from Gujarat to Maharashtra after noting that Ms. Bano had been “coerced to live the life of a nomad and an orphan… the gruesome and horrific acts of violence have left an indelible imprint on her mind which will continue to torment and cripple her”.

articles.title: BJP holds key party meeting in Mathura for Assembly polls
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The party announced the meeting to discuss organisational programmes, booth empowerment, and public welfare benefits, while also outlining electoral strategy and caste-based outreach

Senior BJP leaders from Uttar Pradesh, including Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, attended a key meeting at the Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya Cow Research Institute in Parkham, Mathura, to discuss strategy for the upcoming U.P. Assembly polls.

The party announced the meeting to discuss organisational programmes, booth empowerment, and public welfare benefits, while also outlining electoral strategy and caste-based outreach to counter the Opposition’s renewed pitch.

“One goal, one idea... BJP government again for the third time... Today, in Mathura, the birthplace of Lord Krishna, I participated in a planning meeting with National General Secretary (Organisation) B.L. Santosh, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, and BJP Uttar Pradesh Incharge Shri Vinod Tawde,” wrote Pankaj Chaudhary, U.P. BJP president, on X.

“In the meeting, various important topics, including upcoming organisational programmes, booth empowerment, and providing benefits of public welfare schemes to every household, were discussed in detail. On this occasion, National General Secretary Irani, Deputy Chief Ministers Shri Keshav Prasad Maurya ji and Shri Brajesh Pathak, co-incharges of BJP Uttar Pradesh, Ministers of the State Government, public representatives, and state officials were present,” he added.

State Deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya said the construction of a grand temple at Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi in Mathura will be a major poll issue in the 2027 U.P. elections, and that a grand Krishna temple will be built—through the courts or mutual dialogue, as with Ayodhya.
“If Akhilesh Yadav wants to join us in kar seva, we will take him along too to build a grand temple of Lord Krishna,” said the Deputy CM.

The meeting in Mathura is also significant amid the BJP’s emphasis on Mathura and western Uttar Pradesh. “The BJP holds meetings regularly to discuss organisational programmes, booth empowerment and other issues. articles.title: Tribute to Kartar Singh Sarabha, Punjab free from drugs and unemployment, says CM Mann
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Chief Minister said his government is working to build the progressive Punjab they envision

Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann said on Monday (November 16, 2026) that the greatest tribute to the 19-year-old revolutionary and freedom fighter Kartar Singh Sarabha is to fulfil his dream of a Punjab free from drugs, unemployment, and injustice.

He was speaking after paying tribute to Shaheed Kartar Singh Sarabha on his 111th martyrdom anniversary at his native village, Sarabha, in Ludhiana district. The Chief Minister said his government is working to build the progressive Punjab they envision.

“Shaheed Kartar Singh Sarabha embraced the gallows at the tender age of just 19, proving that courage, conviction and love for the motherland know no age. At a time when youngsters today are planning their futures, this great revolutionary was planning the liberation of the country. He sacrificed his youth, dreams and ultimately his life for our freedom,” he said.

“On November 16, 1915, Shaheed Kartar Singh Sarabha was hanged at Lahore Central Jail along with six other revolutionaries in the First Lahore Conspiracy Case. His fearless commitment to the freedom of the country remains a shining example of patriotism and selflessness,” he added.

As the Punjab 2027 Assembly election approaches, the drug menace has once again become a central campaign issue. In the run-up to the Assembly polls, the major political parties in the fray—the Congress, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD), and the ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)—are making the drug menace a key plank of their campaigns.

While the ruling party has been asserting that eradicating drugs is its “biggest priority,” the Opposition parties have accused the AAP of failing to curb the drug menace and instead patronising the drug trade.

articles.title: Export duty on diesel hiked ₹2.5/litre, ATF ₹1.5/litre, petrol remains nil
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The government late Monday (November 16, 2026) hiked the export duty on diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF) by ₹2.5 per litre and ₹1.5 per litre, whilst keeping the levy on export of petrol unchanged at nil.
Duty rates on petrol and diesel meant for domestic consumption remain unchanged.
The hike in diesel levy assumes added significance as India looks to further up their exports of the vehicular fuel to Europe amid a global supply crunch.
In the upcoming fortnight, diesel exports would draw a levy of ₹14 per litre compared to ₹11.5 per litre mandated for the previous fortnight.
ATF exports would draw a levy of ₹12.5 per litre against ₹11 per litre.

The government has been conducting a fortnightly review of export levies since March 27, in the backdrop of the conflict in West Asia. These are done based on the average international benchmark prices of crude oil, petrol, diesel and ATF observed since the previous review.
This is to ensure the domestic availability of retail fuels by disincentivising exports.

articles.title: U.S. federal court strikes down fixed terms for student, exchange visas
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: In July, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed a policy aimed at preventing international students from staying in the country for more than four years unless they obtained federal approval
A U.S. federal court has struck down a Trump administration proposal to cap the amount of time foreign students, scholars, and journalists can spend in the country on their respective visas.

In July, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed a policy aimed at preventing international students from staying in the country for more than four years unless they obtained federal approval.

Boston federal Judge F. Dennis Saylor delivered a ruling on Monday (November 16, 2026) striking down the DHS proposal as "arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and otherwise not in accordance with law."

"Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity — providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States — that Congress sought to permit and encourage," Judge Saylor said in his ruling.
"The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa programme," he added.
The proposed rule also sought to shorten how long foreign journalists can stay in the country from several years to 240 days – or 90 days for Chinese journalists.
The proposed rule also shortened the grace period – the window to depart after finishing studies or post-completion OPT from 60 days to 30.
For language programmes, there was an aggregate limit of 24 months for stays, including breaks and vacations.
The Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies (FIIDS) welcomed the federal court order.

"Once again, the court has come to the rescue of international students — and, in doing so, has helped protect the future of American science, technology, research, and innovation," said FIIDS President and Chief of Policy and Strategy, Khanderao Kand.

articles.title: News Analysis | Drone warfare leaves no safe zones in Sudan

fullParagraphs: Unmanned strikes are reshaping warfare, disrupting supply lines and expanding the battlefield into previously secure areas. Markets, hospitals, transport hubs, and homes are increasingly targeted, heightening civilian risk amid a deepening humanitarian crisis

On October 18, there was a drone strike on a crowded transport hub near a market in Al-Dibab, a city in the West Kordofan State of Sudan. After ten minutes, a second drone struck the same place, and at least 139 people died in the attack. Eight days later, there was another drone strike in a market in Nyala, the capital city of South Darfur, killing over 100 people, according to the rights group, Emergency Lawyers.

These attacks point to the emergence of a concerning trend in the ongoing civil war in Sudan. What began as a fight for political supremacy between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023 is gradually evolving into a warfare campaign that heavily relies on unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV).

Global & Diplomatic Brief: News Analysis | Drone warfare leaves no safe zones in Sudan. This development underscores India's strategic autonomy and pragmatic engagement in bilateral and multilateral diplomacy.

articles.title: Author Samina Mishra explores borders, identity and citizenship through children’s eyes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The filmmaker and author examines how art and storytelling can open up conversations about society, equality and constitutional values

What do borders mean to a child? Is it a line separating two countries, a language that makes someone feel like an outsider, or the invisible divisions that determine who belongs and who does not? For filmmaker and children’s author Samina Mishra, these questions have informed much of her work with children, particularly those growing up in circumstances where displacement, identity and belonging shape everyday life. Samina, who will be in Visakhapatnam for the Vizag Junior Literary Fest this month, believes that young people must have the space to question the divisions that shape their world.

Her engagement with these ideas took shape through a three-year association with Simurgh Centre in Delhi, where she conducted art workshops with children from Khirkee, a south Delhi neighbourhood home to several Afghan refugee families. The monthly Simurgh Children’s Art Workshop, designed for children aged nine to 15, offered them an opportunity to watch films, discuss their themes and respond through art. For children with limited access to spaces for play, leisure and creative expression, these sessions opened up possibilities for engaging with the world beyond their immediate circumstances.

During the first year, Samina selected short films from different countries, particularly those that communicated visually with little or no dialogue, allowing children from different linguistic backgrounds to participate. One of the films screened was The Present , a Palestinian short about a father and son attempting to buy a gift and the difficulties they encounter at checkpoints.
“It initiated conversations about lines and borders. That is also what my book Lines explores,” she says.

In her workshops for children, the idea of a line extends beyond geographical boundaries. Through discussions and art-based exercises, children examine the many ways people are separated, whether by language, caste, community or circumstances.

The conversations also draw from their experiences of moving to unfamiliar places and negotiating questions of identity and belonging. By encouraging children to approach these subjects through their own experiences, Samina hopes to make larger social questions more accessible.

Her interest in children’s understanding of society formed another project called ‘Hum Hindustani’, a research initiative she conceived and executed, which examines citizenship through the constitutional principles of liberty, equality and fraternity. Part of the Transforming Education for Sustainable Futures (TESF) India network, the project engages children in Grades 6 to 9 across three locations: Shaheen Bagh in Delhi, rural Firozpur in Punjab and Kitab Mahal, a library serving Dalit and Muslim children in Govandi, Mumbai.

Each location represents a distinct social and political experience, from the citizens’ protest at Shaheen Bagh to the farmers’ movement in Punjab and community-led learning initiatives in Govandi. Through arts-based exercises and documentary interviews with children and adults, the project explores how constitutional promises relate to the realities of growing up in different social settings.

“The initiative documents children’s creative responses through artwork and poetry,” says Samina. Its Hum Hindustani Poetry Podcast brings their writing into conversation with writers, artists and educators. Available in English and Hindi, the recordings offer an insight into how young people interpret citizenship through their everyday experiences.

For Samina, the project also addresses the marginalisation of children’s voices in conversations about democracy and society. “While children are frequently discussed in the context of education, welfare and public policy, their own interpretations receive far less attention,” she says and adds, “Children must be recognised as individuals capable of thinking about their rights, relationships and responsibilities.”

Samina, who will be in Visakhapatnam for the Vizag Junior Literary Fest this month, believes that young people must have the space to question the divisions that shape their world.
• Her engagement with these ideas took shape through a three-year association with Simurgh Centre in Delhi, where she conducted art workshops with children from Khirkee, a south Delhi neighbourhood home to several Afghan refugee families. The monthly Simurgh Children’s Art Workshop, designed for children aged nine to 15, offered them an opportunity to watch films, discuss their themes and respond through art. For children with limited access to spaces for play, leisure and creative expression, these sessions opened up possibilities for engaging with the world beyond their immediate circumstances.

articles.title: Keralam’s State Planning Board moots a Partnership Cell for forging a ‘partnership economy’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The proposed cell will focus on forging partnerships among the government, the private sector including the non-resident Keralite community, the local bodies, cooperatives and banks. It will shortlist transaction advisers and review progress quarterly as district-level meetings wrap up by December 12.

In line with the idea of creating a ‘partnership economy’ in a scenario where the State government’s resource-raising abilities are limited, the Kerala State Planning Board will soon have a Partnership Cell to explore investment opportunities by roping in multiple entities including the private sector and cooperatives.

Speaking to The Hindu in connection with Keralam’s upcoming 15th five-year Plan (2027-2032), Planning Board Vice-Chairman K.M. Chandrasekhar said the proposed cell will focus on forging partnerships among the government, the private sector including the non-resident Keralite community, the local bodies, cooperatives and banks.

The concept is founded on the idea that while the State government’s potential to raise financial resources is limited, Keralam as a State has wealth. The Board will short-list transaction advisers whose services can be used for various projects, Mr. Chandrasekhar, who is a former Union Cabinet Secretary, said.

Over the past few weeks, Planning Board officials have been conducting meetings in the districts as part of drawing up the 15th Plan. Meetings have been completed in ten districts and the Board hopes to cover the remaining four by December 12. The heads of the Planning Board’s divisions will be placed in charge of two districts each as part of the Partnership Cell’s activities. Once in three months there will be a plan review.

“The State does not have enough money to carry forward a meaningful development programme. We have already said in the White Paper (’Kerala’s Fiscal Health: A Status Report’ prepared by a team led by Mr. Chandrasekhar earlier this year) that 77% of our revenues go into salaries, interest and pensions. What remains again gets distributed on a number of welfare schemes. The actual expenditure of the State on capital is only about 1.34%. So, how do you generate investment? It’s a very simple economic formula that the more investment you put in the greater will be your return,” he said.

In mid-November, the Board had announced that the 15th Plan would aim to raise Keralam’s gross state domestic product (GSDP) from ₹16 lakh crore to ₹28 lakh crore, achieving a growth rate of 7% per year as opposed to the current 5%. Also, the Plan would be prepared in smart mode, where outcomes are ‘specific, measurable, achievable, result-oriented and time-bound.’

The Planning Board Vice-Chairman pointed to the recently-passed Simplified and Accelerated Regulatory Approvals and Licensing (SARAL) Keralam Bill, 2026, as a major step towards removing needless roadblocks in the path of potential investors.
